entry.title: Setting Up Self-Service SSO in SAP LeanIX with SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS)
entry.content:
If you're running SAP LeanIX today with basic username/password login, or with an older SSO connection that was set up by SAP support years ago, there's a change worth knowing about: SAP LeanIX's legacy SSO service is retired on July 3, 2026, with no extension. In its place, LeanIX now offers self-service SSO configuration - you no longer need to raise a support ticket and wait for SAP to wire up your identity provider. You do it yourself, directly in the Administration area, using SAML 2.0.

I recently went through this end-to-end using SAP Cloud Identity Services - Identity Authentication (IAS) as the identity provider, and I'm sharing the walkthrough here, along with a few things that aren't obvious the first time you do it.

Two SSO Modes - Pick One Before You Start

Before touching any configuration, it's worth understanding that LeanIX gives you two different SSO options, and the one you pick changes what you configure later:

- SSO - Authentication: IAS handles login (authentication), but role assignment and authorization still live inside LeanIX. This is the lighter-touch option if you just want centralized login.

- SSO – Authentication and Authorization: IAS handles both login and role/authorization decisions. This is the option you need if you want to use extended features like Virtual Workspaces or custom roles driven from your IdP.

Decide which one fits your governance model up front - switching later means reconfiguring attributes, not just flipping a toggle.

 Prerequisites

- SSO configuration enabled in your LeanIX workspace (see below if this is your first time).

- Admin access to SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS), with permission to create SAML applications and define attributes. If you don't have this, loop in your IAM or identity team early - you'll need them for the attribute mapping step.

Step 1: Enable SSO Setup in LeanIX

If you've never configured SSO for this workspace before, you'll need to enable it first:

1. In LeanIX, go to Administration → Authentication and SSO.

2. Select one of the SSO authentication types described above.

3. Click Save.

Note: If you already had an SSO connection configured before November 2025, the self-service setup should already be enabled for you - you can skip straight to adding a new identity provider.

Step 2: Add a New Identity Provider in LeanIX

LeanIX allows up to 5 identity provider connections per workspace, which is handy if you're running a phased rollout or supporting multiple IdPs.

1. Go to Administration → Authentication and SSO → Identity Providers.

2. Select the authentication type and click Add Identity Provider.

3. Provide the identity provider details.

4. Click Next.

You'll then need to hop over to IAS to create the matching SAML application.

Tip: If you ever need to change an existing SSO connection's settings, LeanIX doesn't support in-place edits - add a new identity provider with the updated config, verify it works, then delete the old one.

Step 3: Create a SAML Application in IAS

1. In SAP Cloud Identity Services, go to Applications & Resources → Applications.

2. Choose Create.

3. Set:

      Type: SAP LeanIX

      Protocol Type: SAML 2.0

4. Choose Create.

 

Step 4: Exchange Metadata Between LeanIX and IAS

This is the step that establishes trust between both sides - SAML metadata has to flow both ways.

From IAS to LeanIX:

1. In IAS, go to Applications & Resources → Tenant Settings.

2. On the Single Sign-On tab, select SAML 2.0 Configuration.

3. Choose Download Metadata File.

4. Back in LeanIX, upload that metadata file into the identity provider configuration and click Next.

Once you've uploaded the IAS metadata, LeanIX generates its own metadata URL.

 

From LeanIX to IAS:

5. In IAS, go to Applications & Resources → Applications → {Your Application} → SAML 2.0 Configuration.

6. Choose Load from URL.

6. Copy the metadata URL LeanIX just generated, paste it in, and choose Load.

 

Loading via URL saves you from manually populating each field - IAS pulls in everything it needs automatically.

Step 5: Configure the SP-Initiated Flow

One thing to flag clearly: LeanIX only supports SP-initiated SSO IdP-initiated login (starting from your IAS app dashboard) will not work. Users always need to start at the LeanIX workspace URL to trigger the login flow.

1. In IAS, go to Applications & Resources → Applications → [Your Application].

2. Choose Edit.

3. Set the Home URL to your workspace address, e.g. https://{region}.leanix.net/{workspacename}/.

If you're planning to move to a custom subdomain, that's a separate request you raise after SSO is configured - you'll come back and update the Home URL once the subdomain is live.

Step 6: Map the Authentication Attributes

This is the step needs to be performed because the default attributes IAS ships with are not the ones LeanIX expects, and everything here is case-sensitive.

1. In IAS, go to Applications & Resources → Applications → [Your Application] → Attributes.

2. Choose Expand All, then delete every default attribute so the list is empty.

3. Add the following required attributes exactly as shown:

 

Required Attributes

Name

Source

Value

firstname

Identity Directory

First Name

lastname

Identity Directory

Last Name

email

Identity Directory

Email

uid

Identity Directory

Email

4. Back in LeanIX, on the Attributes & Users step, check "I have configured the attributes and assigned users in SAP Cloud Identity Services" and click Next.

Step 7: Test the Connection

Don't skip this - test before you activate.

1. In LeanIX, go to Administration → Authentication and SSO.

2. On the identity provider tile, select Test Configuration.

3. Open the provided URL in a private/incognito browser window and log in with your IdP credentials.

If you can't use a private window (locked-down corporate browser, for example), copy the test URL, log out of LeanIX first, then reuse the URL in your regular browser. A successful test redirects you to IAS for login and lands you back in your workspace afterward.

 

Managing Access via IAS: Role Attributes

Getting SSO working handles authentication - proving who someone is. If you chose SSO – Authentication and Authorization back in Step 1, you also need to hand authorization (what a user can do once logged in) to IAS. That's a separate, optional layer on top of everything above, and it's where a lot of the real access-management value sits.

Step 1: Configure Role Attributes in IAS (Standard Roles)

LeanIX ships with three standard roles - VIEWER, MEMBER, and ADMIN. To manage these externally instead of assigning them by hand inside LeanIX, there are three parts to it: create one group per role, put users in the right group, then map a role attribute to the group's external name.

Create a group for role

IAS has a hard restriction; you can only create one group per SAP LeanIX role attribute. Once you've created, an ADMIN group, that's the only group that grants default admin permissions - every user who needs admin access has to be a member of that specific group. There's also no editing a group after the fact: if you need to change one, you delete it and recreate it.

1. In IAS, go to Users & Authorizations → Groups.

2. Choose Create.

3. Enter the general information, then Next Step.

4. Select the application you created for LeanIX (Step 3 above).

5. Under External Name, enter the role value exactly as it should appear in LeanIX e.g. ADMIN (case-sensitive) this is literally the value LeanIX will read.

6. For Group Type, select userGroup.

7. Choose Next Step, review the summary, then Finish.

Repeat this for MEMBER and VIEWER, so you end up with three groups:

 

External Name

Group Type

VIEWER

userGroup

MEMBER

userGroup

ADMIN

userGroup

 

Step 2: Assign users to the right group

1. In IAS, go to Users & Authorizations → User Management → Groups.

2. Select the group you created.

3. Choose Add to add users, then Add again to save.

Steps 3:  Map the role attribute to the SAML application

This is the step that enables group membership to what LeanIX sees in the SAML assertion.

1. In IAS, go to Applications & Resources → Applications → [Your Application] → Attributes.

2. Choose Add.

3. Configure the attribute:

Name

Source

Value

Role

Identity Directory

Application Groups - External name

4. Choose Save.

With this in place, a user's group membership becomes the single source of truth the role attribute sent to LeanIX just mirrors whichever of the three groups they belong to.

Here's what that looks like coming across in the SAML assertion once it's working:

That role: ADMIN line is the whole point of the exercise - LeanIX reads it straight off the assertion and grants access accordingly, no manual role assignment inside LeanIX involved.

A Few Practical Lessons

A handful of things I'd tell someone doing this for the first time:

- Don't clone an existing SAML application if you're setting up a second workspace or migrating - most IdPs (IAS included) don't clone attribute configuration correctly. Build the new application from scratch.

- Each workspace needs its own SSO connection - with its own Entity ID and Reply/ACS URL - even if several workspaces point to the same underlying SAML application in IAS.

- Case sensitivity on attribute names will silently break login if you get it wrong - firstname is not the same as firstName as far as the mapping is concerned, so copy the table above exactly rather than retyping from memory.

- Test in incognito, every time - An active session in your regular browser will mask configuration issues that a fresh login would catch.

 

Conclusion:

 

 
By moving to self-service SSO configuration with SAP Cloud Identity Services, organizations can take control of authentication and authorization for LeanIX directly. The step-by-step setup covered above walks through the SSO activities required - from enabling SSO, establishing trust with Identity Provider via metadata exchange to mapping the authentication attributes LeanIX expects. There are also a set of activities such as configuring group in IAS to provide the access via SAML 2.0 and enabling custom role attributes for authorization providing via SSO IdP. This will help administrator to manage Identity and access management for LeanIX solution

 

References:

User and Access Management | SAP Help Portal

Configure Access Control Entity Attributes in IAS | SAP Help Portal

entry.title: Automating Time-Bound SAP SuccessFactors RBP Access with Entra ID and Cloud Identity Services
entry.content:
Introduction

What if an HR administrator needs elevated access to SAP SuccessFactors for two weeks? Or an AMS support team member needs temporary access to troubleshoot an issue for an approved support period?

In both cases, access should be approved, time-bound and automatically removed when it is no longer required.

Traditionally, this may involve manually adding users to SuccessFactors Permission Groups and remembering to remove them later. This creates administrative effort and increases the risk of temporary access remaining active longer than intended.

A better approach is to use Microsoft Entra ID for access governance, while continuing to use SuccessFactors Role-Based Permissions (RBP) to control application access. By connecting Microsoft Entra ID with SAP Cloud Identity Services – Identity Authentication (IAS) and Identity Provisioning (IPS), approved group memberships can be provisioned to SuccessFactors Permission Groups automatically.

From Project Experience to Practical Guidance

In a recent SuccessFactors project, I implemented this approach using Microsoft Entra ID and SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS/IPS). It provided an opportunity to work through the complete lifecycle of time-bound SuccessFactors access and see how it can be applied in a real-world implementation.

In this blog, I share the solution approach, key configuration steps and some important implementation considerations.

Note on Microsoft Entra ID Governance

An Entra ID specialist or IAM Engineer is required to configure Access Packages, approval workflows and time-bound access policies in Microsoft Entra ID. The configuration of Entra ID Governance is outside the scope of this blog. This blog focuses on how the configured Entra ID Governance capabilities integrate with SAP Cloud Identity Services and SAP SuccessFactors to enable controlled, time-bound access.

Solution Overview

The solution follows this flow:

Microsoft Entra ID manages who can request access, approval and duration. IAS and IPS handle the identity and group provisioning, while SuccessFactors RBP determines what the user can access.

Prerequisites

Before starting the IAS, IPS and Microsoft Entra ID configuration, ensure the following are available:

  • SuccessFactors: Required RBP Permission Groups and Permission Roles are configured.
  • Cloud Identity Services: IAS is configured for SuccessFactors, and IPS is connected to the required systems.
  • Microsoft Entra ID: Required users, groups, owners and approval structure are defined.
  • Access governance: Approval process and access duration/expiry requirements are agreed.
  • Identity mapping: A consistent user identifier is available across Entra ID, IAS, IPS and SuccessFactors.
  • Access & permissions: Required admin accounts, API permissions and authorizations are available.

Step 1: Configure Microsoft Entra ID to SAP Cloud Identity Services

  • In the Identity Authentication Service (IAS) admin console, provision a new System Administrator account and generate an API Client Secret and assign the required permissions for SCIM REST API operations (READ/WRITE access for users/groups)

  • In Microsoft Entra ID, configure the Enterprise Application SAP Cloud Identity Services using SCIM protocol, targeting the IAS SCIM base URL and authenticating with the generated system credentials.

This allows Entra ID to provision user profiles and group assignment payloads directly to SAP Cloud Identity Services via SCIM.

The screenshots above are only intended to illustrate standard user provisioning from Entra ID to IAS via the SCIM API. Depending on your Entra ID tenant tier (e.g., Microsoft Entra ID P1/P2), the outbound SCIM payload can also include the groups as required for the downstream SuccessFactors transformation scenario.

Reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/saas-apps/sap-cloud-platform-identity-authentication-provisioning-tutorial

Step 2: Configure IAS as the IPS Source

Next, configure IAS as the source system in IPS so that IPS can read the users and group memberships provisioned from Entra ID. For this, establish certificate-based authentication and configure Identity Authentication as the Source System.

  • Source System:
    • In IPS, create a new Source System of type Identity Authentication. Use default transformation.
    • Configure mandatory Properties
  • Authentication & Authorization:
    • Generate a certificate directly within the newly created IPS Source System
    • Download the certificate and assign it to the System Administrator account in IAS (we can use the same administrator account used by Entra ID)

Reference: https://help.sap.com/docs/identity-provisioning/identity-provisioning/identity authentication?q=source+system

Step 3: Configure SuccessFactors as the IPS Target

IPS now needs to be able to update SuccessFactors Permission Groups. For this, establish certificate-based authentication and configure SuccessFactors as the Target System.

  • Target System:
    • In IPS, create a new Target System of type SuccessFactors. Select the IAS source system created in the previous step.
    • Configure the required target properties.
  • SuccessFactors Authentication:
    • Generate a certificate directly from the newly created Target System.
    • In SuccessFactors, Security Center, X.509 Certificate Mapping, map the public certificate to an administrative service user that has permissions to access and manage Role-Based Permission and Permission Groups.

Reference: https://help.sap.com/docs/identity-provisioning/identity-provisioning/target-sap-successfactors

Step 4: Configure the IPS Transformation

The transformation is not simply passing the group membership from IAS to SuccessFactors. The user entity must first be processed by IPS so that IPS can establish the correlation between the source user and the corresponding SuccessFactors target user. Once that correlation exists, resolveEntityIds in the group transformation can resolve IAS group member to the corresponding SuccessFactors userId.

The JSON below represents the Target Transformation JSON used in IPS to map user identities and group assignments to SuccessFactors Permission Groups (Dynamic Groups)

User block:

  • condition: Ensures the transformation only processes user records containing an employeeNumber
  • skipOperations: ["delete"]: Prevents unintentional user deletions in SuccessFactors
  • userId: Maps the SCIM employeeNumber directly to the target SuccessFactors userId

  • replaceFirstString: Trims external naming conventions or internal security prefixes (e.g., SF_GRP_PREFIX_) from displayName so the group name created in SuccessFactors matches the business definition
  • resolveEntityIds: group member resolution

Reference: https://help.sap.com/docs/identity-provisioning/identity-provisioning/transformation-expressions

Step 5: Payload Validation
Upstream Group Assignment in IAS

SCIM group membership payload provisioned from Microsoft Entra ID into SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS).

IPS Transformed User Payload

Target user transformation payload mapping the employee userId (personIdExternal).

The user transformation block must execute so IPS can execute downstream member resolution.

Outbound OData API Payload (DynamicGroup)

Transformed target JSON payload generated for the SuccessFactors DynamicGroup OData API, containing the target groupID, groupName (prefix removed), and resolved member userIds.

Verified SuccessFactors Permission Group

Admin Center view confirming the updated Role-Based Permission (RBP) Dynamic Group reflecting the synchronized Entra ID group membership.

 



Important Implementation Note: SuccessFactors User ID

By default, the SuccessFactors userId is not exposed and mapped directly in standard SAP Cloud Identity Services schemas or default SAP SuccessFactors SCIM API mappings. While employeeNumber in IAS is typically mapped from personIdExternal in SuccessFactors, relying solely on personIdExternal can create challenges in rehire scenarios, where a new userId may be generated). To address this, a separate job can be used to retrieve the SuccessFactors userId and populate it into a custom attribute in SAP Cloud Identity Services. This custom attribute can then be used in the IPS target transformation instead of employeeNumber, providing a reliable way to resolve and maintain the SuccessFactors member userId.

Reference: https://help.sap.com/docs/successfactors-platform/managing-user-information/mapping-between-scim-users-and-odata-user

In this implementation, the SuccessFactors OData API (DynamicGroup) was used to update Permission Group membership. The SuccessFactors SCIM API (Groups) can also be used and the same pattern using resolveEntityIds may be applied to translate member identities, although the target transformation will need to be adjusted to suit the SCIM target schema.

Reference: https://help.sap.com/docs/successfactors-platform/managing-user-information/overview-of-sap-successfactors-workforce-system-for-cross-domain-identity-management-api

End-to-End Testing

Once the configuration is complete, test the complete lifecycle using a test user.

1. Request Access
The user requests the required application or role through Microsoft My Apps and completes the configured approval process.

2. User Group Provisioning in IAS
Once approved, the user's membership in the relevant Entra ID group is provisioned to IAS.

The updated logs from Job Execution in IPS should show the payload sent to SuccessFactors to update the Permission Group membership.

3. User Group Assignment in SuccessFactors
 When the scheduled IPS job runs, the group membership is transformed and provisioned to the corresponding SuccessFactors Dynamic Permission Group. The user should now receive the associated RBP access.

4. Validate expiry
 When the configured access duration expires in Microsoft Entra ID, the user's group membership is removed. The subsequent provisioning cycle processes this change and removes the user from the corresponding SuccessFactors Permission Group.

This completes the access lifecycle without requiring manual removal in SuccessFactors.

 


Conclusion: The Complete Identity Lifecycle

This approach provides a reusable pattern for managing temporary SuccessFactors access through an organisation's existing identity governance framework. Microsoft Entra ID manages the request, approval and access duration, while SAP Cloud Identity Services handles the identity and group provisioning, and SuccessFactors RBP ultimately controls the user's access.

The result is a more controlled and auditable way to provision temporary SuccessFactors access without relying on manual Permission Group administration.

entry.title: Who Just Logged Into My SuccessFactors Instance?
entry.content:
Building a Near-Real-Time Login Alert with IAS, SAP BTP Audit Log Service, n8n, and Gmail

This blog will talk about how to build an n8n workflow that monitors SAP SuccessFactors login events. It connects SAP Identity Authentication, SAP BTP Audit Log Service, n8n, and Gmail to detect a successful login, identify the user and source IP address, optionally enrich the location, and send an email alert automatically.

Why I Built This

This experiment started while I was working through SAP's August Developer Challenge – New Joule Studio. The Week 3 n8n challenge introduced a hands-on workflow exercise, which inspired me to extend the idea into a practical authentication-monitoring scenario against a real SuccessFactors environment.

Instead of stopping with the challenge exercise, I wanted to test a practical question:

What could n8n actually automate around a real SAP SuccessFactors environment?

So I picked a very simple operational scenario:

Whenever someone successfully logs into my SAP SuccessFactors demo instance, can I automatically receive an email showing who logged in, when they logged in, the source IP address, and the approximate location?

I did not want another report that somebody had to remember to check. I wanted an event to trigger the next action.

Someone logs into SAP SuccessFactors
        ↓
SAP Identity Authentication records the event
        ↓
SAP BTP Audit Log Service receives it
        ↓
n8n retrieves and filters the event
        ↓
Source IP is optionally enriched
        ↓
Gmail alert

One of the most important lessons from this build was that a "successful login" event by itself is not enough. The same Identity Authentication tenant can generate authentication events for several applications and technical clients. The key was identifying the serviceProvider value associated specifically with my SuccessFactors tenant.

That discriminator is what allowed the workflow to distinguish a genuine SuccessFactors login from the surrounding authentication noise.

This is not an SAP-delivered SuccessFactors login-alert feature. It is an integration pattern built on SAP authentication and audit capabilities, with n8n acting as the orchestration layer.

What We Are Building

The final architecture is intentionally small:

SAP SuccessFactors
        ↓
SAP Cloud Identity Services
Identity Authentication
        ↓
SAP BTP Audit Log Service
        ↓
Audit Log Retrieval API
        ↓
       n8n
        ↓
Filter actual SuccessFactors login
        ↓
Deduplicate event
        ↓
Optional IP geolocation
        ↓
Gmail alert

The resulting notification can contain:

SuccessFactors Demo Login Detected

User: <USER>
Login Time: <TIMESTAMP>
Source IP: <IP>
Approximate Location: <CITY / REGION / COUNTRY>
Authentication: SAML 2.0
Result: Successful

Prerequisites

Before starting, you need:

  • SAP SuccessFactors using SAP Cloud Identity Services / Identity Authentication for the authentication path you want to monitor
  • Access to the Identity Authentication Administration Console
  • An SAP BTP Cloud Foundry subaccount
  • SAP Audit Log Service access
  • A Cloud Foundry space
  • Space Developer access to that space
  • n8n
  • A Gmail connection in n8n
  • Optional: an IP-geolocation service

I strongly recommend testing this against a demo or non-production SuccessFactors tenant.

Scope note: This pattern monitors authentication events that pass through SAP Identity Authentication. Authentication paths that bypass IAS will not be visible to this workflow. Before treating this as a security control, confirm that the authentication paths you want to monitor actually traverse Identity Authentication.

Part 1 – Build It

Step 1: Confirm That Identity Authentication Sees the Login

Do not start with n8n.

First prove that SAP is generating the authentication event you need.

Open:

SAP Cloud Identity Services → Monitoring & Reporting → Troubleshooting Logs

  1. Open a fresh Incognito/private browser session.
  2. Navigate to your SuccessFactors instance.
  3. Perform a fresh login.
  4. Return to Troubleshooting Logs.
  5. Inspect the events around the exact login time.

In my tenant, the Identity Authentication audit event exposed key/value attributes including:

state
action
category
objectType
caller
cause
additionalAttributes

For authentication activity, useful values can include:

state="successful"
action="login"
category="audit.authentication"
ipAddress="<SOURCE_IP>"
workflow="saml2.0"

In my tenant, the authentication event used the audit.authentication category and exposed values such as successful, login, and saml2.0. Confirm the exact fields and values in your own tenant before building the filter.

Important: Not Every Authentication Event Is a Fresh SuccessFactors Login

IAS can also generate events for previous sessions, token activity, SAML challenges, logout, BTP applications, technical clients, and other connected applications.

So this is too broad:

action = authenticate

We need the event that specifically means:

A user successfully entered this SuccessFactors instance.

Step 2: Connect Identity Authentication Audit Logs to SAP BTP

Open:

IAS → Monitoring & Reporting → Audit and Change Logs → Audit Logs

If you see:

No Auditlog Service Configuration

Identity Authentication is not yet connected to a BTP Cloud Foundry Audit Log destination.

Choose Add and provide the requested BTP subaccount information, including:

  • Tenant ID
  • Region
  • Subdomain, if you want the direct Audit Log Viewer link

The BTP Cloud Foundry region must map to the Identity Authentication region. SAP also notes that the configuration is enabled within approximately the next 15 minutes.

Once the region mapping is configured, verify the target BTP Cloud Foundry subaccount before continuing:

 

Step 3: Find the Real SuccessFactors Login Signature

Open the SAP Audit Log Viewer for the BTP subaccount.

If you receive an authorization error, verify the relevant BTP audit-log authorization assigned to your user. If access was just granted, establish a fresh login session before testing again.

In Audit Log Viewer:

  1. Select security-events.
  2. Reduce the time window around your SuccessFactors login.
  3. Search for successful.

At the BTP Audit Log level, these entries appear as:

audit.security-events

Inside the IAS security-event payload, the authentication event itself can contain:

state="successful"
action="login"
category="audit.authentication"
loginName="<USER>"
mail="<EMAIL>"
ipAddress="<SOURCE_IP>"
workflow="saml2.0"
serviceProvider="<SUCCESSFACTORS_SERVICE_PROVIDER>"

Those two categories are not contradictory:

BTP Audit Log event type
        ↓
audit.security-events

Identity Authentication event inside it
        ↓
audit.authentication

Also inspect your own payload before choosing the user field. Depending on the authentication flow, authenticatedSubject may not yet contain the useful login identity, while attributes such as loginName or mail may be more useful.

Step 4: Identify the SuccessFactors-Specific Discriminator

This is the most important filtering decision in the workflow.

Filtering only on:

state="successful"
action="login"

is not sufficient because the IAS tenant may authenticate several applications.

In my scenario, the most useful discriminator was:

serviceProvider

The SuccessFactors event contained a SuccessFactors-specific service-provider value.

Represent yours as:

<YOUR_SUCCESSFACTORS_SERVICE_PROVIDER>

Do not copy the value from another tenant. Find the value from your own successful login event.

The final matching rule becomes:

state = successful

AND

action = login

AND

category = audit.authentication

AND

serviceProvider =
<YOUR_SUCCESSFACTORS_SERVICE_PROVIDER>

Step 5: Verify the BTP Cloud Foundry Setup

Go to:

BTP Subaccount → Cloud Foundry Environment

Confirm that you have:

  • Cloud Foundry enabled
  • A Cloud Foundry organization
  • At least one space

Then open:

Space → Space Members

Verify that your user has:

Space Developer

SAP documents Space Developer as the prerequisite role for the corresponding space when setting up the Audit Log Retrieval API.

If the cockpit tells you that you must be an org member, remember that BTP subaccount authorization and Cloud Foundry org/space membership are separate authorization layers.

Step 6: Create the Audit Log Management Service Instance

In your Cloud Foundry space, open:

Services → Service Marketplace → Audit Log Management Service

Use:

Service:
Audit Log Management Service

Technical name:
auditlog-management

Plan:
default

Create an instance. For example:

sf-login-audit

Create a service key for the n8n integration. For example:

n8n-key

The service key contains values broadly like:

{
  "url": "...",
  "uaa": {
    "url": "...",
    "clientid": "...",
    "clientsecret": "..."
  }
}

Do not publish the real client secret. Keep it in the n8n credential store rather than in JavaScript, workflow notes, screenshots, or exported examples.

SAP also recommends recreating auditlog-management service-instance bindings and service keys at least every 90 days.

Step 7: Understand the Two Different URLs

This was one of the easiest places to make a configuration mistake.

OAuth Token Endpoint

Take the service-key value:

uaa.url

and use:

<uaa.url>/oauth/token

Audit Log Retrieval Endpoint

Take the top-level service-key value:

url

and append:

/auditlog/v2/auditlogrecords

So conceptually:

OAuth token
    ↓
<uaa.url>/oauth/token

Audit records
    ↓
<url>/auditlog/v2/auditlogrecords

For the non-mTLS client-secret flow, SAP documents OAuth client credentials using the UAA client ID and client secret.

Step 8: Configure OAuth2 in n8n

Create an n8n OAuth2 API credential.

Configure:

Grant Type:
Client Credentials

Access Token URL:
<uaa.url>/oauth/token

Client ID:
<uaa.clientid>

Client Secret:
<uaa.clientsecret>

Scope:
Leave blank unless your environment requires otherwise

 

Keep the client secret inside the n8n credential store.

Step 9: Retrieve the Audit Events from n8n

Add an HTTP Request node and name it:

Fetch SAP Audit Logs

Configure:

Method:
GET

Authentication:
OAuth2 API

URL:
<url>/auditlog/v2/auditlogrecords

Add three separate query parameters.

time_from

{{ $now.minus({ minutes: 10 }).toUTC().toFormat("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss") }}

time_to

{{ $now.toUTC().toFormat("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss") }}

category

audit.security-events

The .toUTC() conversion is intentional. SAP expects time_from and time_to in UTC using the format YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.

Do not add a leading =, unnecessary quotes, or paste all three query parameters into one value.

A successful response contains records with fields such as:

message_uuid
time
tenant
org_id
space_id
category
user
message

Step 10: Filter and Deduplicate the SuccessFactors Login

My Schedule Trigger runs every two minutes, but the API deliberately looks back ten minutes.

Schedule:
Every 2 minutes

Audit lookback:
Previous 10 minutes

The overlap is intentional because SAP states that newly generated audit logs are not immediately accessible for retrieval.

But overlap means the same login can be returned multiple times, so the next node needs to both identify the real SuccessFactors login and suppress duplicate alerts.

Add an n8n Code node after Fetch SAP Audit Logs and name it:

Filter + Deduplicate SF Login

Replace <YOUR_SUCCESSFACTORS_SERVICE_PROVIDER> with the value identified from your own successful login event.

const staticData = $getWorkflowStaticData('global');

staticData.seenLogins =
  staticData.seenLogins || {};

const results = [];
const now = Date.now();

const retentionMs =
  24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;


// Remove old deduplication entries
for (
  const [id, timestamp]
  of Object.entries(staticData.seenLogins)
) {

  if (now - timestamp > retentionMs) {
    delete staticData.seenLogins[id];
  }
}


function extract(text, field) {

  if (!text) return '';

  const regex =
    new RegExp(
      `${field}\\s*=\\s*"([^"]*)"`,
      'i'
    );

  const match =
    String(text).match(regex);

  return match
    ? match[1]
    : '';
}


for (const item of $input.all()) {

  const record = item.json;

  let payload = {};

  try {

    payload =
      typeof record.message === 'string'
        ? JSON.parse(record.message)
        : (record.message || {});

  } catch {

    payload = {};

  }


  const data =
    typeof payload.data === 'string'
      ? payload.data
      : JSON.stringify(
          payload.data || ''
        );


  const searchable =
    `${data} ${record.message || ''}`;


  const state =
    extract(searchable, 'state');

  const action =
    extract(searchable, 'action');

  const category =
    extract(searchable, 'category');

  const serviceProvider =
    extract(searchable, 'serviceProvider');

  const loginName =
    extract(searchable, 'loginName');

  const email =
    extract(searchable, 'mail');

  const workflow =
    extract(searchable, 'workflow');

  const correlationId =
    extract(searchable, 'correlationId');


  const ip =
    payload.ip ||
    payload.ipAddress ||
    extract(searchable, 'ipAddress') ||
    '';


  const isSuccessFactorsLogin =

    state === 'successful' &&

    action === 'login' &&

    category ===
      'audit.authentication' &&

    serviceProvider ===
      '<YOUR_SUCCESSFACTORS_SERVICE_PROVIDER>';


  if (!isSuccessFactorsLogin) {
    continue;
  }


  const eventId =

    record.message_uuid ||

    correlationId ||

    `${record.time}-${loginName}-${ip}`;


  if (staticData.seenLogins[eventId]) {
    continue;
  }


  staticData.seenLogins[eventId] =
    now;


  results.push({

    json: {

      eventType: 'LOGIN',

      eventId,

      correlationId,

      user:
        loginName ||
        email ||
        payload.user ||
        'Unknown user',

      email,

      timestamp:
        record.time ||
        payload.time,

      ip,

      state,

      action,

      category,

      workflow,

      serviceProvider

    }

  });

}


return results;

 

The result can turn dozens of generic security events into one actual SuccessFactors login event.

Important When Testing Deduplication

The example above uses $getWorkflowStaticData('global') for lightweight deduplication.

n8n documents workflow static data as an experimental feature. Static data is not available during manual workflow testing; the workflow must be published and invoked by a trigger or webhook before static data is saved between executions.

So seeing a duplicate login while repeatedly testing nodes manually does not automatically mean the deduplication logic is broken.

For production scenarios where duplicate suppression is security-critical, I would use durable storage such as an n8n Data Table, database, Redis, or another persistent store instead of relying only on workflow static data.

Step 11: Use a Known Historical Window When Debugging

If the Code node returns:

No output data

do not immediately rewrite the parser.

The current rolling window may simply contain no successful SuccessFactors login.

Temporarily query a historical period where you already know a successful login exists:

time_from:
2026-08-20T12:00:00

time_to:
2026-08-20T12:10:00

Run Fetch SAP Audit Logs and then Filter + Deduplicate SF Login.

If the known login appears, your parser is working. Restore the dynamic rolling window afterward.

This separates:

Parser problem

from

No matching login in this time range

Step 12: Do Not Mistake the Audit Log API's Own Login for SuccessFactors

This is a subtle false-positive trap.

The Audit Log Retrieval API itself authenticates using an OAuth technical client, and SAP's own sample audit data shows successful client-authentication events for auditlog-management.

That means a simple search for:

successful login

can match technical-client activity that has nothing to do with an employee entering SuccessFactors.

The SuccessFactors-specific serviceProvider condition is what prevents that false positive.

Step 13: Add Optional IP Geolocation

The filtered event contains the source IP address. You can optionally pass it to an external IP-geolocation service.

For example, an n8n HTTP Request can use a single-IP geolocation endpoint and pass:

{{ $json.ip }}

The response can provide fields such as:

  • City
  • Region
  • Country
  • ISP

Call this Approximate Location, not the user's physical location. VPNs, proxies, corporate gateways, and mobile networks can all affect the observed IP location.

Also review your organization's privacy requirements before sending source IP addresses to an external enrichment provider. For stricter environments, skip this step and keep only the source IP.

Step 14: Send the Gmail Alert

Add the n8n Gmail node.

Use:

Resource:
Message

Operation:
Send

A suggested subject is:

[SF DEMO] Login detected - <USER>

The message can contain:

SuccessFactors Demo Login Detected

User:
<USER>

Login Time:
<TIMESTAMP>

Source IP:
<IP>

Approximate Location:
<CITY>, <REGION>, <COUNTRY>

Authentication:
SAML 2.0

Result:
Successful

n8n's Gmail node supports sending both text and HTML messages.

SAP SuccessFactors Security Alert Email

Step 15: Final Workflow

After removing temporary troubleshooting nodes, the Workflow sequence:

  1. Every 2 minutes, the Schedule Trigger starts the workflow.
  2. Fetch SAP Audit Logs retrieves recent audit events.
  3. Filter + Deduplicate SF Login identifies the relevant SuccessFactors login.
  4. Login Event? allows only matching login events to continue.
  5. IP geolocation optionally enriches the source address.
  6. Gmail - Login Alert sends the notification.

The Login Event?node acts as a gate. Only events that pass the SuccessFactors login filter continue to IP geolocation and email notification.

Final n8n workflow with the Login Event? gate

That is the complete demo solution.

No browser scraping. No custom SuccessFactors extension. The workflow consumes authentication evidence already generated through SAP Identity Authentication and SAP BTP Audit Log Service.

Note: The screenshot retains the broader workflow name used during the demo. This article covers successful login monitoring only; change monitoring is outside the scope of this blog.

Troubleshooting

ProblemLikely Cause What to Check
No Auditlog Service ConfigurationIAS is not connected to the BTP Audit Log destinationConfigure the BTP tenant ID, compatible region, and optional subdomain in IAS Audit Logs
Audit Log Viewer says not authorizedMissing audit-log authorization or stale sessionVerify BTP authorization and establish a fresh login session after role changes
You must be an org memberMissing Cloud Foundry org/space membershipVerify Cloud Foundry membership separately from BTP subaccount authorization
Service creation is not authorizedMissing Space DeveloperCheck Space → Space Members
OAuth failsWrong token endpointUse <uaa.url>/oauth/token, not the Audit Log API host
HTTP 400 / Whitelabel Error PageMalformed query parametersEnsure time_from, time_to, and category are separate parameters and timestamps are UTC
HTTP 501 / filter_category_not_supportedCategory filtering is not supported for the current retention/environment configurationRemove the category query parameter and filter the returned events inside n8n
Code node returns no outputNo matching SuccessFactors login in the current time window, delayed availability, or wrong serviceProvider valueUse a known historical window before changing the parser
Too many successful-login eventsOther applications or technical clients are also authenticatingFilter using the SuccessFactors-specific serviceProvider
Duplicates during manual testingn8n workflow static data does not persist during manual testsPublish the workflow and run it through the trigger, or use durable storage

Part 2 – Production Hardening

Prefer mTLS

The walkthrough above uses the OAuth client ID/client-secret flow because it is easy to reproduce and understand in a demo environment.

For production implementations, SAP strongly recommends mutual TLS (mTLS) using X.509 certificates for auditlog-management. SAP's current documentation also recommends moving existing non-mTLS setups toward the mTLS configuration.

I would therefore treat the client-secret configuration in this article as a learning/demo path rather than my preferred production security design.

Implement Pagination

The Audit Log Retrieval API uses server-side paging.

SAP fixes the page size at:

500 records

When more results are available, the API returns a Paging response header containing a handle. Pass that handle into the next request to retrieve the next chunk.

For a quiet demo tenant the first page may be sufficient. For a busy production tenant, do not assume the first 500 records represent the complete result set.

Poll Responsibly

This workflow polls every two minutes, which is extremely conservative relative to SAP's documented API limits.

SAP currently documents:

  • 8 requests per second per authentication token/tenant on CF-EU10, CF-EU20, CF-US10, and CF-US30
  • 4 requests per second per authentication token/tenant on CF-EU11, CF-EU30, CF-US20, CF-US21, CF-JP10, CF-JP20, and CF-BR10

Requests above the supported rate return HTTP 429.

There is also little value in polling every few seconds because SAP explicitly states that newly generated audit logs are not immediately accessible for retrieval.

Monitor the Monitor

A security-monitoring workflow has an uncomfortable failure mode:

If the workflow stops running, silence can look exactly like "nobody logged in."

For production, configure a separate n8n error workflow beginning with the Error Trigger so workflow failures generate their own alert.

Login Monitor
      ↓ failure
Error Workflow
      ↓
Email / Teams / Incident

For a stronger control, add a heartbeat as well. A watchdog can check whether the login-monitor workflow has executed successfully within an expected period and alert if it has gone silent.

Use Durable Deduplication

For this demo, workflow static data keeps the design simple. For a production security control, use durable state when duplicate suppression matters.

Options include:

  • n8n Data Tables
  • A database
  • Redis
  • Another persistent event-ID store

Understand the Scope Boundary

This design only sees authentication events that reach SAP Identity Authentication.

If a population authenticates through another path that bypasses IAS, this workflow will not see those logins. Validate the end-to-end authentication architecture before using the workflow as a security control.

Think About Alert Design

An email for every normal employee login would become noise in a large production tenant.

More interesting production rules might include:

Privileged administrator login

Repeated failed authentication

Login from an unexpected country

First-seen source IP for an administrator

Login outside support hours

Authentication anomaly followed by a sensitive action

And Gmail does not have to be the final action. The same event could create a ServiceNow incident, notify a Microsoft Teams security channel, feed a SIEM, or trigger another investigation workflow.

Final Thought: The Login Alert Is Only the Beginning

I started with one requirement:

Tell me when somebody logs into my SuccessFactors instance.

But after building it, the more interesting question became:

What else could we automate once SAP events become triggers?

The interesting part was not Gmail. It was the architecture:

SuccessFactors authentication
        +
Identity Authentication evidence
        +
SAP BTP Audit Log Retrieval API
        +
Workflow orchestration
        =
Actionable event

Audit logs are normally something administrators inspect after somebody asks, "Who logged in?"

But the same audit record can become an event source:

Detect
   ↓
Understand
   ↓
Filter
   ↓
Act

This particular workflow does not use an LLM at all.

And that is part of the point.

Not every automation needs AI. But reliable agents will still need events, APIs, workflows, and actions underneath them.

For me, this SuccessFactors login monitor was less about receiving an email and more about exploring that architecture.

Today it watches a login. Tomorrow it could watch something much more important.

In this build, the workflow ends with an email alert, but adding n8n AI nodes powered by GPT, Claude, or Gemini opens possibilities far beyond this use case. I will leave the next one to your imagination.

What SAP event would you automate next?

Disclaimer

This example was created in a demo environment.

The workflow is not an SAP-delivered SuccessFactors feature. n8n and the optional IP-geolocation service are external components.

Before implementing a similar pattern in production, review your organization's security, privacy, credential-management, IP-address handling, network, retention, and monitoring requirements.

entry.title: Named-User Attribution Across BTP Subaccounts: A Two-Hop IAS Token Exchange for Cloud Integration
entry.content:
• The scenario

  • Problem 2: audit anonymization

  • Hop 2: XSUAA jwt-bearer exchange

  • BTP trust configuration

  • Applicability beyond Cloud Integration

  • Conclusion

Service keys are convenient — until a compliance team asks who deployed that iFlow. When a central BTP application manages Cloud Integration across multiple subaccounts using client_credentials, every action appears in the audit log under a technical service principal, and every user effectively holds full admin permissions regardless of their actual role. This post describes a two-hop IAS token exchange that restores per-user RBAC enforcement and named-user attribution without redesigning the platform. It is aimed at BTP architects building integration platforms, AI-driven automation, or multi-tenant orchestration on Cloud Foundry.

The full working implementation is available on GitHub: https://github.com/agnissh/btp-cloud-integration-named-user-propagation

 

Disclaimer: The code in this post and the linked repository is a sample implementation intended to illustrate the pattern. It is not production-ready and does not represent SAP best practices or official SAP guidance. Before using this in a productive environment, apply proper error handling, token caching, secret management, logging, and security review appropriate to your organization's standards.

The scenario

A large enterprise runs Cloud Integration in multiple BTP subaccounts — one per region or business unit — all under the same global account. All subaccounts share a single SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS) tenant as their OIDC identity provider: the orchestrator subaccount (where centralized applications/extensions are hosted) and every target Cloud Integration subaccount each have OIDC trust configured to this same IAS tenant. 

In this case an application built on CAP and SAPUI5 orchestrates integration content across all tenants: developing iFlows from templates, generating test configurations, deploying, and managing lifecycle.

The shared IAS tenant is the key architectural precondition for the pattern described here. XSUAA instances are scoped to their own subaccount — a token issued by the orchestrator's XSUAA is not accepted by a target subaccount's XSUAA. IAS sits above the subaccount boundary: because every subaccount trusts the same IAS tenant, an IAS-issued identity token is portable across all of them. This is what makes cross-subaccount named-user propagation possible without redesigning the platform.

The standard approach: create a Process Integration Runtime service instance (api plan) in each target subaccount, generate a service key with roles like AuthGroup_IntegrationDeveloper, store credentials in a BTP Destination, and call the OData APIs via client_credentials.

This works. But it creates two problems that block enterprise adoption.

Problem 1: authorization bypass

The service key carries broad roles. When the orchestrator uses client_credentials, the resulting token inherits all permissions of that service key regardless of who triggered the action. A user who should only have monitoring access can deploy iFlows because the service key has deploy permissions. The target subaccount's role collections are bypassed entirely.

Problem 2: audit anonymization

Action : DEPLOY
User   : sb-xxxxxxxx!b2341|pi-rt!b2341
Tenant : ci-eu10-prod

No human identity. Compliance blocker .

The fix

With the two-hop token exchange described below, the target XSUAA issues a token scoped to the actual user. The user must have the appropriate role collection assigned in that specific subaccount. If they do not, the Cloud Integration API call returns 403 because the token carries no CI-specific scopes. If they do, the call succeeds and the audit log records their identity. Authorization enforcement and audit attribution restored in one architectural change.

Why this matters for agentic solutions

This pattern becomes critical as organizations adopt AI agents for integration operations:

Use case Why named-user matters

AI-assisted iFlow developmentAgent generates integration flows from natural language. Must operate within the requesting developer's permission boundary — junior devs modify only their packages.
Automated test generationAgent reads iFlow config, generates test payloads, triggers execution. Access policies control which teams test which packages.
Self-healing integrationAgent diagnoses a failed iFlow, proposes fix, human approves redeployment. Redeploy attributed to the approver.

Where an agent already receives an IAS token as part of its calling context, the same two-hop exchange applies without any changes to the pattern described here.

When a single jwt-bearer hop is enough

If the target service runs in the same subaccount as the orchestrator: a single jwt-bearer exchange from the user's XSUAA token works. Same zone, same trust boundary — no IAS intermediary needed.

This breaks for cross-subaccount scenarios. XSUAA instances are zone-isolated — a jwt-bearer token issued by the orchestrator's XSUAA is not accepted by a XSUAA in a different subaccount. IAS solves this because it operates above the subaccount boundary: a single shared IAS tenant across the global account makes it a portable, cross-subaccount identity carrier.

Architecture

btp-solution-diagram

Token exchange flow

The sequence diagram above shows the complete flow. The text below covers only the configuration and code you need — the diagrams tell the story.

sequence-diagram

IAS app dependency configuration

This is the critical manual step that cannot be automated via MTA. In the IAS Admin Console:

  1. Navigate to Applications & Resources → Applications
  2. Select your source application (e.g., "btp-named-user-propagation")
  3. Open the Dependencies tab
  4. Click Add
  5. Select the Cloud Integration provider application — look for the entry that corresponds to your target Integration Suite subaccount (the exact name varies by tenant)
  6. Save

orchestrator-application-config

 

provider-application-setup

cis-orchestrator-dependency-setup

Without this dependency, Hop 1 returns invalid_grant. If the dependency exists but IAS_CLIENT_ID is set to the CF service binding clientid rather than the IAS application clientid, Hop 1 returns JWT aud claim rejected.

Implementation

AppRouter: forward the IAS token

Set the following in your AppRouter module in mta.yaml. The AppRouter then forwards the IAS JWT as an x-identity-token header to the CAP backend on every request.

- name: btp-nup-router
  type: approuter.nodejs
  properties:
    ENABLE_FORWARD_CORPORATE_IDP_TOKEN: true
    SEND_XFRAMEOPTIONS: false
    COOKIES: '{"SameSite":"None"}'
    SESSION_TIMEOUT: 30

xs-security.json: embed IAS token as fallback

When direct header forwarding is unavailable (for example, machine-to-machine calls that bypass the AppRouter), XSUAA can embed the IAS token as a claim inside the XSUAA JWT. The CAP backend can then extract it from xs.system.attributes['ias-token'].

{
  "xsappname": "btp-named-user-propagation",
  "tenant-mode": "dedicated",
  "oauth2-configuration": {
    "system-attributes": ["ias-token"]
  }
}

Resolve IAS token (primary + fallback)

The helper below checks for the IAS token in both locations. The header source is preferred because it carries a fresher token; the embedded claim is the fallback for non-browser flows.

function resolveIasToken(httpReq) {
  const headerToken = httpReq.headers?.['x-identity-token'];
  if (headerToken) return { token: headerToken, source: 'x-identity-token header' };

  const authHeader = httpReq.headers?.['authorization'] ?? '';
  const xsuaaToken = authHeader.startsWith('Bearer ') ? authHeader.slice(7) : null;
  const embedded = extractIasToken(xsuaaToken); // xs.system.attributes['ias-token']
  if (embedded) return { token: embedded, source: 'xs.system.attributes[ias-token]' };

  return { token: null, source: null };
}

Hop 1: IAS app-to-app exchange

Use the IAS service binding credentials bound to the CAP backend (identity service, application plan). The resource parameter identifies the target Cloud Integration provider application as registered in IAS. The returned token is a new IAS JWT scoped to that provider app — it now carries the original user's identity but is acceptable to the target subaccount's XSUAA in Hop 2.

Note on the IAS client: A CF identity service binding is the most convenient way to provision the OAuth2 client, but it is not the only option. Any IAS application with valid client credentials and the app dependency configured will work — including the application that was registered in IAS when you set up the BTP subaccount trust. In that case, retrieve the client ID, secret, and token URL from IAS Admin Console and supply them via environment variables or a BTP Destination instead of a service binding.

async function iasApp2AppExchange(userIasToken) {
  const params = new URLSearchParams({
    grant_type: 'urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer',
    client_id: process.env.IAS_CLIENT_ID,
    client_secret: process.env.IAS_CLIENT_SECRET,
    assertion: userIasToken,
    resource: process.env.IAS_RESOURCE
  });
  const res = await httpsRequest('POST', process.env.IAS_TOKEN_URL,
    { 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' }, params.toString());
  return JSON.parse(res.body).access_token;
}

Hop 2: XSUAA jwt-bearer exchange

Present the IAS token from Hop 1 to the target subaccount's XSUAA token endpoint. The clientId and clientSecret come from the Process Integration Runtime service key stored in the BTP Destination. XSUAA validates the IAS token against its configured OIDC trust, resolves the user's role collections, and returns a scoped XSUAA JWT.

async function jwtBearerExchange(tokenServiceURL, clientId, clientSecret, assertion) {
  const params = new URLSearchParams({
    grant_type: 'urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer',
    assertion
  });
  const auth = Buffer.from(`${clientId}:${clientSecret}`).toString('base64');
  const res = await httpsRequest('POST', tokenServiceURL,
    { 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded', 'Authorization': `Basic ${auth}` },
    params.toString());
  return JSON.parse(res.body).access_token;
}

Result: a token with sub = user@company.com, scoped to the user's role collections in the target subaccount. If the user has no relevant role collection assigned in that subaccount, the subsequent Cloud Integration API call returns 403 — XSUAA still issues the token, but with no CI-specific scopes, and Cloud Integration rejects it at the resource level.

Cloud Integration API call (CSRF required)

Cloud Integration's OData API requires a valid CSRF token on write operations. Fetch it first with a GET, then reuse it on the mutating call. The Bearer token is the XSUAA JWT from Hop 2 — Cloud Integration will record its sub claim in the audit log.

const csrfRes = await httpsRequest('GET', `${url}/api/v1/`,
  { 'X-CSRF-Token': 'Fetch', 'Authorization': `Bearer ${accessToken}` });

await httpsRequest('POST', `${url}/api/v1/DeployIntegrationDesigntimeArtifact?Id='${id}'&Version='active'`, {
  'Authorization': `Bearer ${accessToken}`,
  'X-CSRF-Token': csrfRes.headers?.['x-csrf-token'],
  'Content-Length': '0'
});

Destination configuration

The Destination stores the target Cloud Integration endpoint URL and the Process Integration Runtime service key credentials. The CAP backend reads this config and performs the two-hop exchange manually — the Destination SDK's built-in OAuth2UserTokenExchange does not support the IAS intermediary step.

Name=target-cpi
Type=HTTP
URL=https://abc123.it-cpi020-rt.cfapps.eu10-004.hana.ondemand.com
Authentication=OAuth2UserTokenExchange
tokenServiceURLType=Dedicated
tokenServiceURL=https://mysubdomain.authentication.eu10.hana.ondemand.com/oauth/token
clientId=sb-xxxxxxxx!b2341
clientSecret=xxxxxxxx
# Do NOT add token-type=ias — forces client_credentials, breaks user exchange
Note: Do not add token-type=ias to the Destination. That property forces a client_credentials grant, which bypasses the user token exchange entirely and reverts to technical-user behavior.
Cloud Integration - Service Key Setup 
cloud-integration-service-key

destination-sample-config

BTP trust configuration

Each target Cloud Integration subaccount must have OIDC trust established with the shared IAS tenant (Security → Trust Configuration in BTP cockpit). This is required for Hop 2: the target XSUAA must be able to validate the IAS JWT that arrives as the assertion. Without this configuration, Hop 2 returns unauthorized.

Configuration reference

Component Setting Purpose

AppRouterENABLE_FORWARD_CORPORATE_IDP_TOKEN: trueForwards IAS JWT as x-identity-token
xs-security.json"system-attributes": ["ias-token"]Embeds IAS token in XSUAA JWT (fallback)
IAS Admin ConsoleApp dependency on Cloud Integration providerEnables Hop 1 exchange
BTP Trust ConfigOIDC trust to shared IAS (per target subaccount)Target XSUAA validates IAS tokens (Hop 2)
BTP DestinationOAuth2UserTokenExchange, DedicatedStores target token endpoint + service key creds
Target subaccountRole collection per userEnforces per-user RBAC
CAP backendIAS OAuth2 client credentials (IAS_CLIENT_ID, IAS_CLIENT_SECRET, IAS_TOKEN_URL)Provides client creds for Hop 1. Typically sourced from a CF identity service binding, but any valid IAS OAuth2 client works — including the application already registered for the subaccount trust, provided you obtain its credentials from IAS Admin Console and configure the app dependency there.

Common failure modes

Symptom Cause Fix

x-identity-token missingENABLE_FORWARD_CORPORATE_IDP_TOKEN not setSet property, cf restart
Hop 1: invalid_grantIAS app dependency not configuredAdd dependency in IAS Admin Console
Hop 1: JWT aud claim rejectedIAS_CLIENT_ID set to CF service binding clientid instead of IAS application clientidUse UUID from IAS Admin Console → app → Authentication and Access → Client Authentication
Hop 1: invalid_resourceIAS_RESOURCE env var wrongCheck provider app name in IAS
Hop 2: unauthorizedNo OIDC trust in target subaccountAdd IAS as trusted IdP
API: 403User lacks role in target subaccountAssign PI_Integration_Developer
API: 403 (CSRF)CSRF token not fetchedGET with X-CSRF-Token: Fetch first
Hop 2: invalid_tokentoken-type=ias on DestinationRemove that property

Applicability beyond Cloud Integration

The two-hop exchange is not specific to Cloud Integration. It applies to any service on BTP that satisfies two conditions:

  1. The target service is protected by XSUAA in a separate subaccount and exposes a service key with tokenServiceURL, clientId, and clientSecret.
  2. The target subaccount has OIDC trust established with the same shared IAS tenant.

When both conditions hold, Hop 1 and Hop 2 are identical regardless of what sits behind the XSUAA. The only thing that changes is the API call in step 4 — the CSRF handling, endpoint paths, and required scopes are service-specific.

What this pattern does not cover

CI/CD pipelines do not have a user session. They use client_credentials and the audit log will record the technical service principal. If named-user attribution matters for pipeline deployments — for example, tracing a production deployment back to the approver who triggered it — consider a design where the pipeline calls an approval service that performs the deployment using the approver's token obtained through an interactive authorization step.

Conclusion

The client_credentials pattern trades security for convenience: it collapses all users into one technical identity, bypasses role enforcement in the target subaccount, and produces an audit trail that names a service key rather than a person. The two-hop IAS token exchange closes both gaps. The target subaccount enforces RBAC against the actual user and records their identity in the audit log — without changes to the target service's own configuration.

The pattern is not limited to Cloud Integration. Wherever a XSUAA-protected service sits in a separate subaccount with IAS trust configured, the same two hops apply. The same is true for AI agents: an agent that holds the user's IAS token can perform the exchange and operate within the user's permission boundary, not a shared service principal's.
