entry.title: Managing BTP Role Collections Centrally in SAP Cloud Identity Services
entry.content:
Anyone who governs authorizations in SAP BTP through Role Collections knows the problem: once several subaccounts or a global account are involved, maintaining group membership directly in each individual BTP cockpit quickly becomes unmanageable. A cleaner alternative is to represent Role Collections centrally in SAP Cloud Identity Services (Identity Authentication / Identity Provisioning), manage membership there, and then write the changes back into BTP automatically.

This article walks through the three steps of this pattern and, at the end, covers a subtlety that can cause a hard-to-interpret error in practice if you don't know about it.

Step 1: Importing Role Collections from BTP into IAS

The first step is to set up an Identity Provisioning job that uses SAP BTP XS Advanced UAA (Cloud Foundry) as the source system and the Local Identity Directory (i.e., the IAS's own directory service) as the target system. This job reads BTP's Role Collections as groups and creates them as groups in IAS — including their existing members.

This step doesn't require any special, customized transformation — the default job is sufficient. The one property that matters is ips.application.id, which must be maintained in both the source system (BTP) and the target system (IAS). Only this makes the imported groups get created in IAS correctly as so-called Authorization Groups — that is, groups that are unambiguously tied to a specific application, rather than generic, free-floating groups with no application context. This association becomes important later, in step 3, when writing back, since it lets you target these groups specifically via the isApplicationSpecificGroup() function.

After a successful run, the Role Collections exist in IAS as Authorization Groups.

Step 2: Assigning Members

From this point on, the actual administration happens: in the Identity Authentication admin console, you open the imported groups and, under the "User Members" tab, add or remove users — through the UI as usual, via the SCIM API, or in combination with additional rule-based assignments through your own transformations. The advantage: this assignment happens centrally in IAS, regardless of how many BTP subaccounts — or the global account — the respective Role Collection actually exists in.

Note: SAP has Group Nesting and Composite Role support on the roadmap for Q4. Hopefully these will turn out to be a real game changer here, since the assignGroup target variable available today in transformations is currently the limiting factor for scenarios like this one.

Step 3: Provisioning the Groups Back into BTP

In the third step, the direction reverses: now the Local Identity Directory is the source, and the respective BTP environment (subaccount or global account, again via the XSUAA connector) is the target. This job writes the membership lists maintained in IAS back into the corresponding Role Collections.

  • We additionally built in the option to pick up further groups through a filter (customgroup.filter), instead of limiting the job to a fixed, explicitly configured set of groups.

The group transformation for the write direction looks, in principle, like this:

{
  "condition": "isAttributeWithOptionalPrefix($.displayName, xsuaa.group.prefix) && (isRegularGroup() || isApplicationSpecificGroup()) && (('%customgroup.filter%' === 'null') || ($.displayName =~ /%customgroup.filter%.*/))",
  "mappings": [
    {
      "sourcePath": "$.displayName",
      "targetPath": "$.displayName",
      "targetVariable": "entityIdTargetSystem",
      "functions": [
        {
          "function": "replaceFirstString",
          "condition": "isAttributeWithMandatoryPrefix(@, xsuaa.group.prefix)",
          "regex": "%xsuaa.group.prefix%",
          "replacement": ""
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "sourceVariable": "entityIdTargetSystem",
      "targetPath": "$.id"
    },
    {
      "sourcePath": "$.members",
      "preserveArrayWithSingleElement": true,
      "optional": true,
      "targetPath": "$.members",
      "functions": [
        { "function": "resolveEntityIds" }
      ]
    },
    {
      "constant": "USER",
      "preserveArrayWithSingleElement": true,
      "optional": true,
      "targetPath": "$.members[*].type"
    }
  ]
}

What matters here is the entityIdTargetSystem variable: since IAS doesn't know a Role Collection's internal BTP ID, the (optionally prefix-stripped) group name is used as a stable correlation key instead. Identity Provisioning is meant to use this key to find the matching, already-existing Role Collection in the target system and update its members — rather than accidentally creating a new, duplicate Role Collection.

The Subtlety: scim.group.unique.attribute

This exact correlation step can produce an error that looks contradictory at first glance:

error=The request to create an entity has failed with: 409 Conflict
The attempt to retrieve the existing entity from the target system was unsuccessful. More than one entity found

The puzzling part: the Role Collection in question demonstrably exists only once in BTP — a look at the BTP cockpit under Security → Role Collections shows no duplicate entry. Yet Identity Provisioning reports, when writing, that it found more than one matching entity.

The reason lies in how Identity Provisioning correlates by default: it queries the target system via a SCIM filter (GET /Groups?filter=displayName eq "<name>") to check whether the group already exists. In the SCIM Groups implementation of SAP BTP XS Advanced UAA (Cloud Foundry), however, this filter parameter isn't reliably honored — the query simply returns the complete, unfiltered group catalog of the zone, regardless of the filter value. As soon as the zone contains more than one group (practically always the case for a global-account zone with its default role collections), Identity Provisioning automatically gets back more than one result on every correlation request and, for safety, aborts with the 409 error described above instead of risking an incorrect update.

You can verify this yourself with two direct API calls against the same interface: a GET /Groups?filter=... always returns every group in the zone regardless of the filter, while a direct, path-based call GET /Groups/{id} — where id, in this case, equals the group's plain-text name — reliably returns exactly one result.

The fix is to explicitly tell Identity Provisioning to use the direct, path-based lookup for correlation instead of the broken filter search. This is controlled by the target-system property:

scim.group.unique.attribute = id

Since id in this scenario equals the group name computed via entityIdTargetSystem anyway, Identity Provisioning reliably and unambiguously finds the existing Role Collection through it and simply updates its member list — instead of creating a new entity or aborting with a conflict error.

Practical Note

This characteristic of the SCIM Groups interface generally affects every target system of type SAP BTP XS Advanced UAA (Cloud Foundry) — that is, every individual subaccount as well as the global account. It's therefore worth setting scim.group.unique.attribute = id from the outset on every such target system, rather than waiting for the error to show up in yet another subaccount. As with any change to a production transformation, a test run in a sandbox environment with a single, clearly scoped group is recommended beforehand.

Summary

The pattern — import Role Collections from BTP, maintain membership centrally in IAS, write changes back — works reliably once correlation on the write-back uses the ID rather than a filter search that, in practice, isn't always dependable. The scim.group.unique.attribute = id property is the key piece that turns a seemingly unsolvable conflict error into stable, working provisioning.

entry.title: Expanding SCIM API Support for SAP Sales & Service Cloud Version 2/ESM: Replicating External Users
entry.content:
Note: This blog post is a follow-up to the original announcement — Introducing SCIM API for SAP Sales & Service Cloud v2: Seamless User Sync — which introduced SCIM-based provisioning for users of type Employee. The enhancement described here extends that capability to support the External user type.
 

Introduction

When we introduced SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) API support for SAP Sales & Service Cloud Version 2, ESM, the initial release focused on provisioning users of type Employee — enabling organizations to automate the full identity lifecycle of their internal workforce through SAP Cloud Identity Services.

With the latest enhancement, now extends this capability to support External users. Organizations can provision and manage non-employee users — such as partners, contractors, or external collaborators — through the same SCIM-based identity lifecycle processes. As a result, these users are created and managed as External Business Users in SAP Sales Cloud Version 2, SAP Service Cloud Version 2, SAP Enterprise Service Management (ESM), and Utilities solutions built on SAP Service Cloud Version 2.

 

What Is New?

The SCIM API for User Management has been enhanced to support replication of userType = External.

When a user is maintained as an external user in the source identity provider — such as SAP Cloud Identity Services - Identity Authentication (IAS) — the user type information can now be propagated to downstream SAP CX applications through SCIM-based provisioning via SAP Identity Provisioning Service (IPS). The user is then created and managed as an External Business User in the target solution.

This enhancement is supported for:

  • SAP Sales Cloud Version 2
  • SAP Service Cloud Version 2
  • SAP Enterprise Service Management (ESM)
  • Utilities solutions built on SAP Service Cloud Version 2

No additional configuration is required beyond what was already established for Employee user provisioning. The userType attribute in the SCIM payload drives the classification at the target.

How It Works

The provisioning flow follows the same architecture established for the Employee user type:

  1. Source: A user is created or updated in SAP Cloud Identity Services - Identity Authentication (IAS), or a connected identity directory, with userType set to External.
  2. Propagation: SAP Identity Provisioning Service (IPS) reads the user record and transmits it to the target system using the SCIM 2.0-based connector (connector version 4).
  3. Target: SAP Sales Cloud Version 2, SAP Service Cloud Version 2, ESM, or a Utilities solution receives the SCIM payload and provisions the user as an External Business User.

As with the Employee flow, this enhanced connector does not require SAP Cloud Integration, supports PATCH operations for incremental updates, and handles conflict resolution automatically.

Availability

The Replicate External User Type in SCIM API feature is generally available as an informational enhancement and is activated by default. The availability date is 18 August 2026

Key Benefits

Automated User Lifecycle Management

Organizations can automate onboarding, updates, and deprovisioning of external users through a centralized identity management platform.

Improved Governance

External users are clearly distinguished from employees, helping organizations maintain accurate user records and comply with security policies.

Reduced Administration Effort

Manual user maintenance across multiple systems is minimized, reducing operational overhead and human error.

Consistent Identity Across Systems

The external user classification remains consistent from IAS to SAP Sales Cloud, SAP Service Cloud, ESM, and Utilities applications.

Better Scalability

As partner ecosystems grow, organizations can onboard large numbers of external users through standard SCIM provisioning mechanisms.

Final Thoughts

The introduction of External User Type replication through the SCIM API is a valuable enhancement for organizations using SAP Sales Cloud, SAP Service Cloud, SAP Enterprise Service Management, and Utilities solutions. By enabling seamless provisioning of contractors, partners, consultants, and other non-employee users from IAS, SAP simplifies identity management while improving governance and operational efficiency.

entry.title: Extending Case Approvals in SAP Sales & Service Cloud v2 + ESM: Using Business Roles for Multi-Users
entry.content:
This blog post is a continuation of: Assigning a Custom Party Role to a Case for Approvals in SAP Sales & Service Cloud v2 + ESM

Introduction

The previous blog post walked through how to create a Custom Party Role, add it to a Case Party Schema, and wire it into an Autoflow approval — a clean and effective pattern for routing a case to a named approver.

But what happens when your business scenario requires more than one approver? What if an entire team needs to approve a case, and that team membership changes over time?

SAP Sales & Service Cloud v2 (SSC v2) and ESM do not have a native Branch or Approval Hierarchy construct the way some other products do. There is no built-in concept of "send to a department" or "broadcast to a group approval pool." You cannot pick a Business Role directly in the Approval Rule as a recipient group — the approval framework works with individual people assigned to the case.

This extension blog describes a practical pattern to bridge that gap:

Use a Business Role in SSC v2 as the governed container of approvers. Sync its membership from IAS via IPS over SCIM. Populate a non-unique Custom Party Role on the Case with all members of that Business Role. Then use the Case Approval flow to route to all those party role members simultaneously.

The result: a fully dynamic, centrally governed multi-user approval — without needing a branch or hierarchy model.

The Problem: No Branch, No Hierarchy, But Multiple Approvers Needed

In SSC v2/ESM case approvals, the approval process resolves its recipients from people assigned to a specific party role on the case. This works well for a single approver — assign one person to the "Line Approver" party role, and the approval goes to them.

However, real-world scenarios often require:

  • A team of approvers where any one member can take action (e.g., a support management pool)
  • A scenario where all members must approve (e.g., a compliance sign-off)
  • A quorum approval (e.g., at least 2 out of 5 approvers must accept)

And critically: approval team membership changes. People join, leave, change roles. Hardcoding names in configuration is not maintainable.

The answer lies in combining three capabilities:

  1. Business Roles in SSC v2 — as a group of approvers with a meaningful identity
  2. IAS User Groups + IPS SCIM provisioning — for centralized lifecycle management of who is in that group
  3. BTP Extensibility for Assignment of Users to Case from Business Role
  4. Non-unique Custom Party Role on the Case — as the runtime carrier of multiple approvers that the approval flow reads

Architecture Overview

IAS (Identity Authentication Service)
  └── User Group: "CASE_APPROVERS_GRP1"
       ├── User A
       ├── User B
       └── User C
          │
          │  IPS SCIM Sync (Business Role provisioning)
          ▼
SSC v2 / ESM
  └── Business Role: Z_CASE_APPROVERS_GRP1
       ├── User A (assigned this Business Role)
       ├── User B (assigned this Business Role)
       └── User C (assigned this Business Role)
          │
          │  Manual or Automated Party Assignment(BTP Extension)
          ▼
  Case → Custom Party Role: Z_GRP_APPROVER (non-unique)
       ├── User A (Party on Case)
       ├── User B (Party on Case)
       └── User C (Party on Case)
          │
          │  Autoflow → Approval Action
          ▼
  Approval Tasks sent to User A, User B, User C
  (All / Any One / At Least X — configurable)

Why This Pattern Works Without a Branch or Hierarchy

ChallengeHow It's Solved
No group/branch concept in approvalsBusiness Role acts as the group container; its members are loaded into a non-unique party role on the case
Approval team changes over timeIAS group membership is updated → IPS SCIM sync propagates changes to SSC v2 Business Role → Next case uses the updated team
Different cases need different approval groupsCreate one Business Role + Custom Party Role per approval group; populate the right one on each case based on conditions
Need any-one or all-must-approve semanticsControlled by the Approval Rule setting — no process redesign needed
Hardcoded user names in configurationNo user names anywhere in config — only role/group names

Summary

This pattern extends the Custom Party Role + Autoflow approval approach with a scalable, centrally governed layer. By treating a Business Role as the approval group, syncing its members from IAS via IPS over SCIM, and surfacing them on the case through a non-unique Custom Party Role, you unlock multi-user approval semantics in SAP SSC v2 / ESM — without needing any branch, hierarchy, or hardcoded user configuration.

The result is an approval flow that is:

  • Dynamic — membership changes in IAS flow through automatically
  • Flexible — supports any-one, all-must, or quorum approval modes
  • Maintainable — no user names in process configuration
  • Governed — IAS is the single source of truth for who approves what

Related blogs:

  • Assigning a Custom Party Role to a Case for Approvals in SAP Sales & Service Cloud v2 + ESM
  • Introducing SCIM API for SAP Sales & Service Cloud v2
  • Expanding SCIM API Support for SAP Sales & Service Cloud Version 2/ESM

entry.title: Why Manually Created Users Lose their Roles After SCIM Replication in SSCv2 +ESM— And How to Fix It
entry.content:
The Situation

Identity and access management in modern enterprise environments often involves a mix of provisioning strategies. In SAP's Sales & Service Cloud v2 (SSCv2) & SAP Enterprise Service Management (ESM), it is common to find tenants where some users are created manually by administrators while others are provisioned automatically through SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management). This hybrid approach seems harmless — until you run a SCIM replication job and discover that manually created users have silently lost all of their assigned roles.

This is not a random glitch. It is a predictable, reproducible behavior rooted in how SCIM-enabled tenants manage role assignments — and understanding it is the first step to preventing it.

The Problem

In a SCIM-enabled SSCv2 tenant, users who were manually created (i.e., not provisioned through SCIM) and had business roles manually assigned to them lose those role assignments whenever a SCIM replication process runs — even though these users are not managed by SCIM at all.

What makes this particularly puzzling is that the Cloud Identity Service (CIS) logs show no record of updates to those manually created users during the replication run. From the system's perspective, nothing happened — yet the roles are gone.

How to Reproduce It

The issue is entirely reproducible. Here is the sequence of events that triggers it:

  1. Create a user manually in SSCv2 (outside of any SCIM provisioning flow).
  2. Assign one or more business roles to this user directly in SSCv2.
  3. Create a second user via SCIM provisioning from the Cloud Identity Service (CIS).
  4. Assign the same roles to the SCIM-managed user through CIS.
  5. Execute the SCIM replication process.
  6. Check the manually created user's role assignments.

Result: The manually created user's role assignments have been removed. The SCIM-managed user's assignments are intact. The CIS logs contain no trace of any action against the manually created user.

Why This Happens: The Root Cause

The behavior is not a bug in the traditional sense — it is a consequence of how role replication works in a SCIM-enabled tenant.

In SSCv2, when SCIM is enabled, the authoritative source for role assignments is Identity Authentication Service (IAS), not SSCv2 itself. The replication flow works as follows:

  • Roles are replicated from SSCv2 to IAS via replication jobs.
  • User-role assignments are replicated from IAS back to SSCv2 via those same jobs.

This means that during a replication run, SSCv2 does not selectively update only SCIM-managed users. Instead, it synchronizes role assignments based on what IAS reports. If a role is assigned to a SCIM-managed user in IAS, that assignment gets written to SSCv2. But because the manually created user has no corresponding record in IAS, the replication job effectively overwrites the role assignment state for that role — removing it from any user not represented in the IAS replication payload.

The silence in the CIS logs is explained by the same mechanism: CIS did not act on the manually created user. The removal is a side-effect of the IAS-driven synchronization overwriting what SSCv2 holds locally.

The Fix: Make Manually Created Users SCIM-Managed

The resolution is straightforward once the root cause is understood: manually created users need to become SCIM-managed users.

The recommended approach is to:

  1. Replicate the manually created users to IAS — either by re-creating them through the SCIM provisioning flow or by synchronizing them into IAS via the appropriate identity provisioning job.
  2. Allow IAS to replicate them back to SSCv2 so that SSCv2 recognizes them as SCIM-managed identities.

Once a user is SCIM-managed, the replication process treats their role assignments as part of the IAS-controlled state. Role assignments will no longer be removed during replication — they will instead be preserved and managed consistently alongside all other provisioned users.

What This Means in Practice

If your SSCv2 tenant is SCIM-enabled, the following rules of thumb apply:

ScenarioRisk
User created manually, roles assigned manuallyHigh — roles will be lost on next replication
User created via SCIM, roles assigned via CIS/IASSafe — roles are managed within the replication loop
User migrated to IAS and replicated back to SSCv2Safe — user is now SCIM-managed

The key principle: in a SCIM-enabled tenant, IAS is the source of truth for role assignments. Any role assignment that exists only in SSCv2 — without a corresponding entry in IAS — is at risk of being overwritten during the next replication cycle.

Recommendations

  • Audit your tenant for manually created users who have business roles assigned. These are the users at risk.
  • Do not mix provisioning strategies for the same set of roles. If a role is managed via SCIM, assume that all assignments for that role will be governed by the IAS replication process.
  • Migrate manually created users to IAS before the next replication run if they need to retain their role assignments.
  • Establish a governance policy that requires all new users in SCIM-enabled tenants to be created through the provisioning pipeline, not manually.
  • Monitor replication logs proactively — the absence of entries in CIS logs does not mean nothing changed in SSCv2.

The Golden Rule: SCIM Is a Day 1 Decision

If SCIM will ever be used in your SSCv2 tenant — even in the future — it must be architected from Day 1.

This is not a configuration preference. It is a foundational architectural decision with production consequences. Here is why:

Scenario RiskLevel Consequence
SCIM enabled before any user creationNoneAll users are provisioned consistently via IAS
SCIM enabled after manual users already existHighFirst replication job silently removes role assignments
Manual users migrated to IAS before next replicationMediumRecoverable — but requires careful, urgent remediation
Manual users NOT migrated before replication runsCriticalUsers lose access in production, no CIS log trace

Even if SCIM is not required at go-live, if there is any possibility it will be introduced later — plan for it now. The cost of retrofitting the provisioning model after manual users are established far exceeds the effort of doing it correctly from the start.

Summary

The loss of role assignments for manually created users in SSCv2 is not a random failure — it is the predictable outcome of a SCIM-enabled tenant architecture where IAS owns the user-role assignment state. The fix requires aligning manually created users with the provisioning model: replicate them to IAS and back to SSCv2, making them SCIM-managed. Once that alignment is in place, the replication process will preserve their role assignments rather than silently remove them.

If you are operating a hybrid environment where both manual and SCIM-provisioned users coexist, this issue is likely already affecting you. Addressing it proactively — before the next replication job runs — is far less disruptive than recovering from unexpected access loss in production.

 

Flow 1: The Problematic Scenario — SCIM Not Planned From Day 1

This is what happens when SCIM is introduced or enabled after users have already been created manually in SSCv2+ESM.

Key Insight: The damage is silent. CIS logs show nothing. The role removal is a side-effect of IAS overwriting SSCv2's local role assignment state — leaving no audit trail pointing to the affected users.

Flow 2: The Correct Approach — SCIM Planned From Day 1

This is the recommended architecture when going to production. SCIM must be the only provisioning channel from the very beginning.

entry.title: Configuring Different IAS Account Activation Email Templates for Employees and Onboardees
entry.content:
Organizations using SAP SuccessFactors Employee Central and SAP SuccessFactors Onboarding often provision both Employees and Onboardees into the SAP Cloud Identity Services, Identity Authentication (IAS) user store through an automated identity provisioning process. Although both user populations are created within the same identity repository, their access journeys and communication requirements differ significantly.

Employees who do not use a corporate identity provider for Single Sign-On (SSO) solution typically require an account activation email that enables them to set their initial password and access the relevant SAP applications. The email should contain employee-specific messaging and clear instructions for activating the account and accessing the required applications.

Similarly, Onboardees require an account activation email that allows them to set their initial password and access SAP SuccessFactors. However, their email communication should also include onboarding-specific messaging and instructions relevant to their pre-hire and onboarding activities.

To provide a seamless and personalized user experience, organizations may need to configure separate activation email templates for Employees and Onboardees. This ensures that each user type receives relevant instructions and tailored communication when their account is provisioned in SAP Cloud Identity Services.

In this blog, we explain how organizations can leverage IAS email templates to tailor account activation communications to the specific needs of Employees and Onboardees, providing a consistent and personalized identity onboarding experience.

 

Steps to Configure Custom Email Template Sets in SAP Cloud Identity Services for Employees and Onboardees
  1. Access the administration console->Application & Resources->Email Templates.

 

     2. Create separate custom email template sets for Employees and Onboardees. Choose Add, enter an appropriate name for the template set, and then save your changes.

      b. Open the HTML version of the default template. Copy its content into a new file, customize the content and formatting for the applicable Employee or Onboardee population, provide an appropriate file name, and save it in .html format both employee and onboardee. You may use HTML online editor to prepare the HTML format.

           b. From the list on the left, select the relevant Employee or Onboardee email template set.

            c. Choose Add Language, complete the required fields in the pop-up window, and upload the corresponding .txt and .html template files created in Step 3.

            d. Choose Save to add the customized email template to the selected template set.

5. Identify the Email Template Set IDs

Once created, each email template set is assigned a unique ID. To identify this ID, select the relevant template set from the list and review the URL displayed in the IAS administration console. The URL follows this pattern:

6. Configure the Target System in Identity Provisioning

  b. Locate and select the target system corresponding to the Identity Authentication tenant used in the provisioning flow from SAP SuccessFactors.

  1. Open the Transformations tab and switch to the JSON Editor view.

Locate the JSON mapping where the target path is emailTemplateSetId, and specify the relevant email template set ID as the constant value.

Replace <email-template-set-id> with the unique ID of the appropriate Employee or Onboardee email template set created in the Step 5.

Employee

Expected Output

When a new Employee is created or an Onboardee is registered in SAP SuccessFactors and subsequently provisioned to SAP Cloud Identity Services, Identity Authentication (IAS), each user population receives its respective customized account activation email.

By selecting the activation link provided in the email, Employees and Onboardees can activate their accounts, set their initial passwords, and access the relevant SAP  application. This approach ensures that each user population receives tailored communication and appropriate access instructions throughout the account activation and onboarding process.

entry.title: Who Still Has Access to My SAP BTP Subaccount?
entry.content:
Reconciling SAP BTP Shadow Users with SAP Cloud Identity Services Using n8n 

Removing Identity and access is one of the most important parts of the identity lifecycle. 

When a user becomes inactive in SAP Cloud Identity Services, the expectation is usually that the user should no longer retain unnecessary access in connected systems. But how do we verify that the expected deprovisioning has actually happened in an SAP BTP subaccount?

That question led me to build this n8n workflow:

Can I retrieve users from SAP Cloud Identity Services and SAP BTP, compare them using their email addresses, and identify BTP users whose IAS identity is inactive or missing?

The workflow retrieves users from both systems through OAuth-protected APIs, normalizes the API responses, compares the users by email address, and generates a CSV report containing the invalid users.   

I also added an optional branch that can delete an invalid BTP user. That branch is intentionally deactivated by default and should only be used after appropriate validation and approval if needed.

This blog will talk about how to build an n8n workflow that could automate user reconciliation.

Why I Built This

Provisioning solutions are normally designed to move identities from a source system to target applications.

But successful provisioning does not automatically answer this question:

Does the target system still contain users who should no longer be there?

For one user, this can be checked manually:

Search for the user in SAP Cloud Identity Services. Check whether the identity is active. Search for the same user in the SAP BTP subaccount. Compare the two records. Record the result.

This approach is manageable for one or two users, but it becomes repetitive and error prone as the user population grows.

I did not want to download two files and maintain a collection of spreadsheet formulas. I wanted a repeatable workflow that could retrieve the current records, apply the same matching logic every time, and produce a file that could be reviewed. 

Provisioning tells us what should have happened. Reconciliation helps us verify what actually exists in the target platform.

Scope note: this pattern only sees identities that actually traverse IAS. If a population is provisioned into BTP through some other path / IGA tools, this workflow won't catch drift there - confirm your own provisioning paths before treating this as a complete control.

What We Are Building

The workflow is intentionally simple. SAP Cloud Identity Services and BTP users are retrieved and normalized separately, after which BTP users are compared against IAS using the normalized email address. The n8n workflow contains the following nodes: 

Schedule Trigger
  ↓
Get IAS Users
  ↓
Normalize IAS Users
  ↓
Get BTP Users
  ↓
Normalize BTP Users
  ↓
Compare and Find Invalid Users
  ↓
Filter Invalid Users
  ↓ (Kept)
  ├── Convert to File (CSV export — audit evidence)
  └── Delete Invalid BTP User (Deactivated) — disabled by default

An optional BTP deletion branch is connected after the invalid-user filter, but it remains disabled by default. The reporting flow can therefore be tested independently without deleting the user.

Prerequisites

Before starting, you need:

  • SAP Cloud Identity Services Tenant
  • IAS Technical system with user read permission 
  • SAP BTP Cloud Foundry Subaccount 
  • An XSUAA Service instance and service Key
  • n8n self-hosted or on a trial (community edition is free to self-host indefinitely for internal use) 

I am using SAP BTP Trial platform and n8n trial (community edition) for this scenario.

Authentication Design

Both API integrations use OAuth-based authentication in this workflow. Of course, you can use Basic authentication for IAS API call.

 IAS Authentication

I have created technical system in IAS Administration console and assigned required access. The technical system provides the client credentials needed by n8n to request an access token.

The IAS user endpoint follows this pattern:

GET https://<ias-tenant>.accounts.ondemand.com/scim/Users

The Identity Directory API exposes SCIM resources for users, groups, and custom schemas.

BTP Authentication

For SAP BTP Cloud Foundry, I used an XSUAA service key.

The XSUAA REST APIs support programmatic administration of security artifacts, including users, roles, and role collections. An XSUAA instance using the appropriate API access plan provides the URL and credentials required for the REST calls.

 

The service key provides values such as:

Client ID
Client Secret
OAuth URL
API URL

In my US10 trial environment, the BTP user endpoint is:

GET https://api.authentication.us10.hana.ondemand.com/Users

The endpoint is region-specific, so should use the API URL provided by own XSUAA service configuration.

Part 1 – Build It

Step 1: Define the Reconciliation Rules

Before creating the comparison logic, I defined the possible outcomes.

Valid user

A BTP user is classified as VALID when:

The BTP user has an email AND exactly one IAS user has the same normalized email AND The IAS user is active

The resulting reason code is: IAS_USER_ACTIVE

Invalid user

A BTP user is classified as INVALID in either of these cases: No IAS user has the same email

Result: IAS_USER_NOT_FOUND

Or:

One IAS user has the same email AND The IAS user is inactive

Result: IAS_USER_INACTIVE

This distinction matters because a data-quality problem should not automatically become a deletion decision.

Step 2: Retrieve IAS Users

The first HTTP Request node is named: Get IAS Users

The node calls the IAS Identity Directory SCIM endpoint:  

GET https://<ias-tenant>.accounts.ondemand.com/scim/Users

The access token is obtained through the OAuth credential configured in n8n. A simplified IAS user from my test looked like this:

The IAS SCIM interface supports user retrieval and filtering through attributes such as emails.value. It also supports pagination using parameters such as startIndex and count.

Step 3: Normalize IAS Users

The IAS response is passed to: Normalize IAS Users

This is an n8n Code node using JavaScript. The normalization step reduces every IAS user to the fields required for reconciliation:

The normalization logic:

  • Reads the SCIM Resources array
  • Selects the primary email when available
  • Falls back to the first populated email
  • Removes leading and trailing spaces
  • Converts the email address to lowercase
  • Preserves the IAS user ID
  • Preserves the IAS active status as a Boolean

Step 4: Retrieve BTP Users

The next HTTP Request node is: Get BTP Users

For my Cloud Foundry trial environment, it calls: 

GET https://api.authentication.us10.hana.ondemand.com/Users

A simplified BTP user from the trial looked like this:

Step 5: Normalize BTP Users

The BTP response is passed to: Normalize BTP Users 

This Code node creates a consistent representation of each BTP user:

The email-selection logic follows this order:

  1. Use the primary email when available.
  2. Otherwise, use the first populated value in emails[].
  3. If the email array is empty, use userName when it contains an email address.
  4. If needed, use externalId when it contains an email address.

Step 6: Why I Compared Email Instead of Username 

It depends on Application subject Name identifier - BTP username could be such as Global UserID, Email, LoginName, UserID etc. But email will be same in both IAS and BTP.

The IAS record contained:

IAS userName: test.user04

The BTP record contained:

BTP userName: testuser04@invalid.example

A direct username comparison would classify these as different users.

The email values, however, were the same:

IAS emails[].value: testuser04@invalid.example

BTP emails[].value: testuser04@invalid.example

For this reason, the workflow compares users using a normalized version of:  emails[].value and The normalization applies: 

String(email ?? '') .trim() .toLowerCase();

This means the following values are treated as equal:

TestUser04@Invalid.Example
testuser04@invalid.example

Step 7: Compare and Find Invalid Users

The node first creates an index of the normalized IAS users: 

Normalized email
↓
IAS user record

Each BTP user is then checked against that index.

For the test user, the workflow found:

BTP user exists: Yes
BTP active: true
IAS email match: Yes
IAS active: false
IAS match count: 1

The result was:

The BTP account is active, but the corresponding IAS identity is inactive. The workflow therefore sends the record to the invalid-user branch. Specific reason codes make the CSV report easier to understand and troubleshoot.

Step 8: Filter Invalid Users

The comparison results are passed to: Filter Invalid Users. The filter keeps records where: validationStatus = INVALID

This includes:

IAS_USER_INACTIVE

IAS_USER_NOT_FOUND

Users classified as VALID are removed from the exception path.

Step 9: Generate the CSV Report

I used "convert to File" node to store the generated invalid user's list so that I can review and delete later after validation.

The output destination can be changed to OneDrive, SharePoint, Google Drive, SFTP, or another controlled repository.

Step 10: Optional Deletion of Invalid BTP Users

A second branch is connected after: Filter Invalid Users.  The branch contains: Delete Invalid BTP User

The node is deactivated by default. When This node is activated, the node can issue a request conceptually similar to:

DELETE https://api.authentication.us10.hana.ondemand.com/Users/<BTP_USER_ID>

The operation uses the BTP user ID returned by the API.

The user ID is safer for targeting the technical record than using the email address alone.

Testing Final Workflow 

Let's see IAS User's list. As I am using trial account, so it is easy count users and remember user's status. 

Here is BTP Users list who has been login. You might notice the difference in BTP user because I did not login in BTP applications using that id.

I will run the n8n workflow without enabling Delete invalid BTP user node. 

Workflow run successfully and provided all invalid user's list in CSV file

Let's check how CSV looks like. 

In CSV, you can check why users are marked as invalid as either user is not active in IAS or does not exist in IAS anymore. 

To delete user

I will enable Delete Invalid BTP User node

Once I will execute this workflow, user should be deleted from BTP subaccount. 

Workflow run successfully.

And users are deleted in subaccounts as well.

As we save invalid records in CSV, you can review how many users are invalid and deleted.

Troubleshooting 

 

Problem

Likely Cause

 What to Check

IAS normalization returns no users

The API response is stored as a JSON string under data.

inspect typeof item.json.data 

The diagnostic output shows thousands of data keys

Object.keys() was called on a string instead of a parsed object.

JavaScript returns character positions: 0 1 2 3

IAS and BTP users do not match

The comparison is using userName.

Compare IAS emails[].value with BTP emails[].value

The BTP email has primary: false

The normalization accepts only an email where primary is true.

Use the primary email when one exists. Otherwise, use the first populated value in the email array.

Every BTP user appears to be missing from IAS

The IAS response was not parsed

IAS totalResults

The deletion node does not execute

The node is deactivated.

active the node for execution

 

Part 2 – Production Hardening

Prefer certificate-based auth over client secrets where it's supported

Client credentials with a shared secret work fine for a POC, but a long-lived secret sitting in a credential store is still a static value someone could leak or need to rotate. Where the target API supports mTLS/X.509-bound OAuth clients, that's the stronger option for a production reconciliation job.

Use least-privileged credentials

The reconciliation path should use read-only permissions wherever possible.

The deletion operation should use a separate, tightly controlled credential rather than sharing the same credential used for reporting.

Keep credentials in the n8n credential store. Do not place client IDs, client secrets, access tokens, or authorization headers in:

  • Code nodes
  • Workflow notes
  • Screenshots
  • CSV files
  • Exported templates
  • Source-control repositories

Recheck IAS before deletion

The user’s status may change between the original comparison and the deletion action.

Before deletion, call IAS again using an email filter: emails.value eq "<candidate-email>"

The deletion should stop if: 

The IAS user is now active
Multiple IAS users match
The IAS API call fails
The IAS response cannot be parsed
The BTP user ID no longer matches
The email has changed

Protect special accounts

Some identities should not pass through a generic deletion rule:

  • Emergency accounts
  • Break-glass administrators
  • Technical users
  • Integration users
  • Service accounts
  • Tenant administrators
  • Privileged support users
  • Accounts used for business continuity

These identities should be excluded or routed to a separate review process.

Implement Pagination

This is the most important known limitation. 

The IAS SCIM API supports pagination through values such as: startIndex, count, totalResults, itemsPerPage

The same completeness check must be applied to the BTP endpoint.

The intended process is:

Request the first page
↓
Read totalResults
↓
Calculate the next startIndex
↓
Request the next page
↓
Combine the results
↓
Stop when all users have been retrieved

Without pagination, a valid IAS identity located on a later page may not be present in the n8n comparison data.

The workflow could then incorrectly classify the corresponding BTP user as:

IAS_USER_NOT_FOUND

For that reason:

The deletion branch should not be activated for a production population until complete pagination has been implemented and tested for both IAS and BTP.

Monitor the reconciliation workflow

A failed reconciliation can create a misleading result.

If the workflow stops running, no exception report is generated. That silence could be mistaken for a clean environment.

A production implementation should include:

  • An n8n Error Trigger workflow
  • Failure notification
  • Last-success monitoring
  • Retrieved-user count monitoring
  • Alerts for unusual count changes
  • Execution logs
  • A heartbeat or watchdog process

Preserve an audit trail

For each execution, retain: 

Execution timestamp
IAS tenant or environment
BTP subaccount
IAS totalResults
Normalized IAS user count
BTP totalResults
Normalized BTP user count
Valid user count
Invalid user count
Review user count
CSV filename
Deletion enabled or disabled
Deletion result
Error details

The report contains identity information, so it must be protected according to the organization’s security, privacy, and retention requirements.

 

Final Thought 

I started with one question:

Does every user in my SAP BTP subaccount still have an active identity in SAP Cloud Identity Services?

The workflow can now answer that question for my trial environment.

The same pattern could be extended to:

  • Reconcile users across multiple BTP subaccounts
  • Identify privileged users with inactive identities
  • Detect unexpected identity-provider origins
  • Create ServiceNow review tasks
  • Notify a Microsoft Teams security channel
  • Maintain reconciliation evidence in an IAM governance platform
  • Track unresolved deprovisioning exceptions
  • Detect technical users mixed with employee identities

Not every IAM control requires a large implementation.

A small, clearly bounded workflow can still make identity differences visible and provide useful evidence. The key is knowing where automated reporting ends and where controlled remediation begins.

What other SAP BTP identity reconciliation scenarios would you automate?

Disclaimer

This workflow was created and tested in an SAP trial environment using one controlled test identity. 

It is not an SAP-delivered BTP user-reconciliation capability. n8n is an external workflow orchestration platform.

The current workflow does not implement complete pagination for IAS or BTP. The workflow should therefore not be used for production deletion until pagination, approval, revalidation, exclusion rules, exception handling, monitoring, and recovery procedures have been implemented and tested.

The Delete Invalid BTP User node is deactivated by default and must be deliberately enabled.

Before adopting a similar pattern in production, review the organization’s requirements for:

  • Identity governance
  • Joiner, mover, and leaver processing
  • Change approval
  • Privileged-access protection
  • API credential management
  • Personal-data handling
  • Audit logging
  • Data retention
  • Incident management
  • Recovery and rollback

Do not delete a BTP user solely because the user appears in a generated CSV. Revalidate the identity and use an approved IAM lifecycle or administrative process.

References

  • SAP Cloud Identity Services, Identity Directory API
    Identity Directory SCIM API and technical-system authorization prerequisites. Identity Directory API | SAP Help Portal
  • SAP BTP, Administration APIs of the Authorization and Trust Management Service
    Overview of APIs for users, roles, role collections, identity providers, and security settings. Accessing Administration Using APIs of the SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service | SAP Help Portal
  • n8n, Convert to File
    Converting workflow data into CSV and other file formats. Convert to File | Nodes | n8n Docs

entry.title: Principal Propagation from BTP to S/4HANA Public Cloud: Configuration Notes and Open Questions
entry.content:
Principal Propagation from BTP to S/4HANA Public Cloud: Configuration Notes and Open Questions

Upfront disclaimer: I have not yet run this end-to-end in a live landscape. What follows is the configuration path I've assembled from SAP Help, a handful of community posts, and my own reading of how the pieces connect. I'm posting it before testing because I couldn't find a single place that covers the Build Work Zone angle properly, and I'd rather have it corrected by people who've actually done it than sit on half-finished notes. Treat this as a starting point, not a verified runbook. If you spot something wrong, please say so in the comments, and I'll update the post.

The problem

We have BTP applications, mostly HTML5 apps surfaced through Build Work Zone, calling S/4HANA Public Cloud APIs. Today that goes through Communication Arrangements with a communication user, which works fine but means every request hits the backend as the same technical account. No per-user authorisation checks, no useful audit trail, and awkward conversations when someone asks who actually changed the purchase order.

So: principal propagation. And the first thing to internalise is that there is no Cloud Connector option here. Public Cloud has no X.509 principal propagation the way an on-premises system does. OAuth 2.0 SAML Bearer Assertion is the path, and as far as I can tell, it's the only one.

How the flow actually works

It took me a while to get the mental model right, and I think this is where a lot of the confusion comes from:

  1. The user logs into Work Zone and gets a JWT from XSUAA (or via your IAS trust).
  2. The HTML5 app calls the backend through the managed approuter, which passes the user token to the Destination service.
  3. The Destination service builds a SAML assertion, puts the user's identity in the NameID, and signs it with the subaccount's Destination Trust certificate.
  4. It sends that to the S/4 OAuth token endpoint. The communication user's credentials authenticate the client here.
  5. S/4 validates the assertion, resolves the NameID to a business user, and returns a token carrying that user's authorisations.

The key point, and the thing I got wrong at first: the communication user is the OAuth client, not the identity being propagated. The business user is the subject. You need both, and they're unrelated objects.

Check this before you configure anything.

Open the Communication Scenario for the API you're targeting and confirm OAuth 2.0 appears as a supported inbound authentication method.

Many SAP-delivered A2X scenarios only offer Basic and X.509. If OAuth 2.0 isn't listed on the scenario, it won't be selectable on the Communication Arrangement either, and principal propagation is off the table for that API. From what I can gather, this is the single most common reason people report that it "doesn't work" when their config is actually fine.

If your scenario doesn't support it, your options are a Custom Communication Scenario built in ADT wrapping your own service, or finding a different standard scenario.

I'd genuinely like to know from anyone who's surveyed this: is there a list somewhere of which standard scenarios support OAuth 2.0 inbound? I've been checking them one at a time, and it's tedious.

S/4HANA Public Cloud configuration

Maintain Communication Users. Create one, save the password somewhere sensible. It becomes the client secret later.

Communication Systems. New system, then:

  • Host Name is your BTP subaccount subdomain
  • Tick OAuth 2.0 Identity Provider
  • Upload the certificate you exported from BTP Cockpit under Connectivity → Destinations → Destination Trust → Export (comes down as a .pem)
  • Copy the CN value from the uploaded certificate into the OAuth 2.0 SAML Issuer field.

That last step is easy to miss because the field does not populate itself. The certificate details render on screen, the CN sits right there, and nothing prompts you to copy it across.

There's a bigger trap sitting behind this one. You upload the Destination Trust certificate, not your XSUAA or IAS SAML metadata. My instinct was to register the identity provider, because that's the mental model everywhere else. But the assertion isn't signed by your IdP. The destination service signs it. If you've configured IAS as your subaccount trust and you upload the IAS metadata here, the assertion will be rejected, and the error message will not tell you why.

Communication Arrangements. Bind the scenario, the system and the user together, then set the inbound user's authentication method to OAuth 2.0. Once you save, the arrangement shows an OAuth 2.0 Details section containing the token endpoint, the SAML audience and the scope. Copy those exactly; don't reconstruct them by hand.

The BTP destination

Property Value

AuthenticationOAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion
URLhttps://my<tenant>.s4hana.cloud.sap/sap/opu/odata/sap/<SERVICE>
audienceS/4 tenant URL with no path, as shown in the arrangement
clientKeycommunication user name
tokenServiceURLhttps://my<tenant>-api.s4hana.cloud.sap/sap/bc/sec/oauth2/token
tokenServiceURLTypeDedicated
tokenServiceUsercommunication user name
tokenServicePasswordcommunication user password
nameIdFormaturn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress
userIdSourceemail
authnContextClassRefurn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:PreviousSession
scopefrom the arrangement, e.g. API_BUSINESS_PARTNER_0001
compactAssertiontrue

Watch the token service host. It carries an -api suffix and is not the same host as the service URL.

One more thing on this table. Do not use the SystemUser property. SAP has deprecated it, and if it's set your propagation quietly collapses into a fixed technical user. Everything appears to work, the calls succeed, and the wrong name shows up in the backend. That's a nasty one to chase.

The Build Work Zone bits

This is the part I couldn't find written down anywhere in one piece.

Add HTML5.DynamicDestination: true to the destination. Without it the HTML5 app can't resolve the destination at runtime through the managed approuter.

Keep the destination in the same subaccount as the Work Zone site. Because the assertion is signed by that subaccount's Destination Trust certificate, and S/4 trusts exactly that certificate, a cross-subaccount setup breaks the chain.

Don't confuse this with HTML5.ForwardAuthToken. That property forwards the raw JWT and belongs to a different pattern (typically a CAP or Node backend). It has nothing to do with the SAML bearer exchange, and setting it here won't help.

And the user has to reach Work Zone through the identity provider whose email matches their S/4 business user. If your Work Zone SSO runs through IAS or Entra and the email on the S/4 business user is different, the assertion will be structurally valid, and the user lookup will still fail.

Identity mapping, which I suspect is where most of the pain lives

With userIdSource: email, S/4 looks up a business user by email address on an exact match. Which means:

  • The person needs an actual Business User in S/4, not just a communication user
  • Their email in S/4 has to match their email in BTP/IAS exactly
  • They need business roles covering the business catalogue behind the OData service

That third point deserves emphasis. Principal propagation enforces real authorisations, which is the entire reason you're doing it. A propagated user with no role gets a clean 403, and from the BTP side that looks identical to a broken propagation setup.

There's a commercial angle here too, and I'd flag it early with stakeholders rather than late. Every propagated user needs an S/4 business user and appropriate roles. If the plan was to let a few hundred Work Zone users read order data, the licensing conversation looks very different from the technical-user integration it's replacing. Worth raising before you build.

If you can't get email alignment, the alternative appears to be userIdSource: user_name with nameIdFormat: ...nameid-format:unspecified, mapping to the S/4 user ID instead. I haven't tried this variant.

Testing and error decoding

Check Connection in the cockpit only proves the endpoint is reachable. It does not exercise the SAML flow at all, which I found misleading. To actually test the exchange, you want to call the Destination service find API with a user token attached:

GET https://destination-configuration.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/destination-configuration/v1/destinations/<DEST_NAME>
Authorization: Bearer <client_token>
X-user-token: <user_jwt>

If authTokens[] comes back populated, the exchange worked. Then check the S/4 side to confirm which user actually arrived, because a successful exchange with the wrong subject is a real failure mode.

Errors I'd expect and what I think they mean:

Symptom Likely cause

invalid_grant, assertion rejectedSAML Issuer field empty or not matching the certificate CN, or wrong certificate uploaded
unauthorized_clientCommunication user credentials wrong, or the arrangement isn't set to OAuth 2.0
invalid_scopeScope doesn't match what the arrangement published
Token issues are fine, then 403 on the API callUser resolved correctly but has no business role for that catalogue
Token issues fine, wrong user in the backendSystemUser is set, or userIdSource is mismatched
Worked for months, then broke everywhere at onceDestination Trust certificate rotated and needs re-uploading to the Communication System.

That last row is one to put in the operations runbook now. The subaccount signing certificate has a finite validity, and nothing on the S/4 side warns you when it expires. I'd expect the failure to arrive as a total outage with no obvious trigger.

An alternative I'm still weighing

If you're fanning out to several backends, or the identity has to survive a hop through middleware, routing via Integration Suite with the SAML bearer flow on the outbound adapter would centralise the trust configuration in one place. It costs you a hop and a subscription, but it also means one place to fix when certificates rotate.

For a single Work Zone to S/4 path, I don't think it's justified. For a landscape with several BTP apps and multiple ERP tenants, I suspect it is. Interested in whether anyone has made that call in either direction and regretted it.

Sources

  • Principal Propagation from SAP Build Process Automation workflow to S/4HANA Public Cloud, which is recent and screenshot-level on the S/4 configuration
  • OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion Flow with the SAP BTP Destination Service, S/4HANA Cloud, older, but it has the full destination JSON and the clearest explanation of Provider Name versus assertionIssuer
  • SAP Help: Scenario: User Propagation from the Cloud Foundry Environment to SAP S/4HANA Cloud, and the Set Up Authentication for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Extensions PDF

Over to you

I'll update this post once we've run it in our own landscape. In the meantime, if you've implemented this:

  • Did the Destination Trust certificate catch you out, or is that just me reading it wrong?
  • Is there a reliable way to see which standard communication scenarios support OAuth 2.0 inbound without opening each one?
  • How are you handling the business user and licensing side at scale?

entry.title: Identity and Access Management with Microsoft Entra, Part IV: Integration with SAP Cloud IAG
entry.content:
This scenario extends the architecture introduced in part III by shifting responsibility for provisioning SAP role assignments from SAP Cloud Identity Services (CIS), Identity Provisioning, to SAP Cloud Identity Access Governance (IAG). Microsoft Entra ID Governance manages the access package and its assignment lifecycle, while SAP IAG applies SAP-specific approval workflows, risk controls, and downstream role provisioning. The scenario introduces the new SAP IAG connector in Microsoft Entra and Microsoft Azure Key Vault for securely storing the credential when calling the SAP IAG REST API.

 

Note 📢

Interested in connecting with us and discuss your SAP and Entra scenario? Then join the SAP and Microsoft identity teams at SAP TechEd 2026 in Berlin, and add hands-on session XP263 to your event agenda, where you will learn how SAP Cloud Identity Services, SAP Cloud Identity Access Governance, and Microsoft Entra work together to unify user lifecycle management and governance across SAP and third-party application.

Scenario Overview

The architecture for part IV builds on the identity provisioning scenario introduced in part III of this blog series. Microsoft Entra ID remains the central service ("source of authority", SOA) for identity data, and SAP CIS continues to receive users from Microsoft Entra and provisions them to downstream SAP target systems, such as the SAP system on-premises in the corporate network shown in figure 1.
Figure 1: Scenario Overview

 

However, responsibility for provisioning application access to the SAP backend system changes. In part III, SAP Cloud Identity Services, Identity Provisioning created the backend roles as groups in Microsoft Entra configured as a target system, and translated group memberships provisioned with the Entra SCIM-based SAP CIS provisioning connector into role assignments in the SAP backend system.

In this new scenario, SAP IAG takes over responsibility for governing and provisioning the user’s role assignment to the SAP backend system. Instead of directly translating a Microsoft Entra group assignment into an SAP role assignment, Microsoft Entra now requests access to an SAP IAG business role. SAP IAG processes the access request, applies the configured approval workflow and access controls, and provisions the underlying technical role to the target SAP backend system.
This separation allows each platform to focus on its core capabilities:
  • Microsoft Entra ID Governance provides the entitlement catalogs, access packages, request policies, and the user-facing Microsoft My Access portal.
  • SAP IAG provides SAP business roles, SAP-specific access request workflows, access analysis, risk evaluation, mitigation controls, and provisioning to connected SAP applications in the Cloud and on-premises.
  • SAP CIS maintains the shared user identities and supports identity synchronization between Microsoft Entra and SAP IAG.
  • SAP BTP connectivity service and SAP Cloud Connector provide the technical connection from SAP IAG to the SAP backend system on-premises.
From all components and configurations marked as "new" in figure 1, the SAP IAG tenant is the most important addition to the architecture in this scenario. SAP IAG maintains the business roles that can be requested through Microsoft Entra and maps those business roles to technical roles in connected SAP applications.
In the example scenario, the SAP IAG business role BR_EPM contains the technical role SAP_BC_EPM_DEMO for the SAP ABAP system A4H. This business role is included in a new Microsoft Entra access package SAP EPM IAG and requested by the user Linda Larson. Microsoft Entra does not provision the underlying ABAP role directly. Instead, Microsoft Entra creates an access request in SAP IAG by calling the SAP IAG Access Request Service API. SAP IAG processes the request and, after the configured workflow has completed successfully, provisions the technical role to the target system.
SAP CIS Identity Provisioning remains part of the wider landscape, particularly when SAP IAG connects to supported cloud applications through Identity Provisioning proxy systems. However, SAP IAG now governs the access decision and orchestrates the provisioning operation for the requested SAP business role.
For this integration, Microsoft Entra ID Governance introduces an SAP IAG connector. The connector establishes the integration between Microsoft Entra entitlement management and the SAP IAG tenant. The connector enables administrators to:
  • Add an SAP IAG tenant as a resource to a Microsoft Entra entitlement management catalog
  • Discover SAP IAG business roles
  • Add SAP IAG business roles to Microsoft Entra access packages
  • Create SAP IAG access requests when an access package is assigned
  • Initiate removal requests when an assignment expires or is revoked
  • Retrieve the processing status of SAP IAG access requests
All of the actions above will be executed in the exercises of this blog series scenario. The connector communicates with SAP IAG through the Access Request Service REST APIs and authenticates by using OAuth 2.0 client credentials which require a secure storage option offered by the Azure Key Vault service to store the SAP IAG API OAuth client secret used by the SAP IAG connector. When configuring the connector in Microsoft Entra, the administrator selects the Azure subscription, Key Vault, and secret. The SAP IAG client ID, OAuth token URL, and SAP IAG API URL are configured as additional connector properties coming from the service key created for the SAP IAG API service instance in the SAP BTP subaccount.
 
SAP CIS remains essential to this scenario. Microsoft Entra provisions users to the Identity Directory in the SAP CIS tenant through SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management, RFC 7644). These users and their identifiers are subsequently synchronized into the SAP IAG repository. The Microsoft Entra user's globally unique object ID is mapped to the SAP Global User ID to provide a stable identity correlation across Microsoft Entra, SAP CIS, and SAP IAG. Manager information must also be synchronized when SAP IAG workflows use the user’s manager as an approver. The scenario therefore governs role access for existing users who must already exist in SAP CIS and in the SAP IAG repository before Microsoft Entra submits the SAP IAG access request.
The target SAP applications must be registered and connected to SAP IAG. The provisioning mechanism depends on the application type:
  • For an on-premises system like the SAP Application Server ABAP, SAP IAG uses an SAP BTP destination, the SAP Connectivity service, SAP Cloud Connector, and the required BAPI or RFC interfaces.
  • For supported cloud applications, SAP IAG can use SAP Identity Provisioning proxy systems and the IPS_PROXY destination configured in the BTP subaccount.
The five steps shown in the scenario diagram of figure 1 illustrate the complete access governance process:
  1. Microsoft Entra provisions the users required in SAP IAG (Linda Larson, Tina Johnson & your Entra administrator user) and their SAP IAG roles as group memberships to SAP CIS through the existing enterprise application and SCIM provisioning connection (Note: inbound- or HR-driven provisioning of the test users in this scenario from SAP SuccessFactors to the corporate Active Directory and from there to Entra does not change from the scenario in part III of this blog series). The provisioning configuration must synchronize the Microsoft Entra object ID of the users as the SAP Global User ID. Manager information must also be synchronized if the SAP IAG workflow uses manager-based approval. In this scenario, Tina Johnson is assigned in Active Directory as the manager of Linda Larson and can approve Linda's access request in SAP IAG. After provisioning from Entra to SAP CIS is complete, the relevant SAP IAG synchronization jobs must import the user, groups, and identifiers from SAP CIS into SAP IAG's user repository. All users must be available in SAP IAG before an access request can be submitted from Microsoft Entra.
  2. Linda Larson opens the Microsoft My Access portal and requests the SAP EPM IAG access package. The access package is maintained in a Microsoft Entra entitlement management catalog and contains the SAP IAG business role BR_EPM.
  3. The SAP IAG connector calls the SAP IAG APIs and creates an access request for the user and selected business role. SAP IAG validates the request and that the user exists in its repository.
  4. SAP IAG processes the request according to the workflow and governance configuration of the SAP IAG tenant. Depending on the organization’s configuration, processing can include manager approval, segregation of duties (SOD) analysis, critical access analysis, assignment of mitigation controls and other steps. In this scenario, Tina Johnson as the manager of Linda Larson needs to approve Linda's access request. Microsoft Entra governs eligibility for the access package and its assignment lifecycle. SAP IAG governs the SAP-specific role assignment and applies SAP-specific risk and compliance controls.
  5. After the SAP IAG workflow has completed successfully, SAP IAG provisions the business role to the connected target applications. In the scenario, the business role BR_EPM contains the technical role SAP_BC_EPM_DEMO for the ABAP system A4H. SAP IAG uses the configured SAP BTP destination to reach the target system through SAP Cloud Connector and invokes the required BAPIs. The result is the assignment of SAP_BC_EPM_DEMO to Linda Larson's user in the SAP backend system.

For a live demo, check out episode #307 of the SAP on Azure video podcast, where @Holger-Bruchelt and I go through the scenario step by step.

Microsoft Entra continues to manage the lifecycle of the access package assignment. If the assignment expires or is revoked, Microsoft Entra uses the SAP IAG connector to initiate a removal request. SAP IAG processes that request and deprovisions the corresponding role from the target system. As part of the following exercises, the Microsoft Entra tenant administrator removes Linda's assignment to the SAP EPM IAG access package to test deprovisioning in the scenario.
