entry.title: SAML 2.0 SSO: Why an SAP Cloud Identity Service broker wins over a direct corporate IdP connection
entry.content:
Introduction

With many organizations moving away from SPNEGO as a Single Sign-On (SSO) pattern, SAML 2.0 (SAML2) is getting more and more popular. Especially considering the administrative efforts to keep Kerberos Authentication alive in a hybrid setup (with Active Directory and EntraID), moving to SAML2 as an authentication protocol is often the more practical choice.

In this Blog post, I will show

  • the benefits of implementing a SAML2-based SSO to an on-premise S/4HANA system with multiple clients (Mandanten) by use of SAP Cloud Identity Service (as an identity broker) and a corporate Identity Provider (IdP).
  • how this setup can help you abstract away the complexity on the corporate IdP side, compared to a direct corporate IdP connection.

Identity Broker vs. direct IdP Connection

For understanding the benefit of using SAP Cloud Identity Service as a layer of abstraction in your SSO setup, let's look at the following drawings. First, let's look at how a direct connection from your S/4HANA system to the corporate IdP would look like: 

Connecting 3 systems (D4H, Q4H and P4H) with 3 clients (Mandanten) per system directly to the corporate IdP would require 9 (3x3) SAML2 applications on the corporate IdP side. This often comes with a scalability problem, as in most companies these SAML2 applications are maintained by separate teams (often times there is an identity team and some sort of SAP operations team). Configuring these applications correctly, having them maintained by a different team and onboarding new applicaitons requires coordination across teams and can be very time consuming. 

Now let's look at the setup using SAP Cloud Identity Service as an Identity Broker for the system landscape:

Connecting D4H, Q4H and P4H via the SAP Cloud Identity Service only requires one SAML2 application on the corporate IdP side. SAP Cloud Identity Service abstracts the configuration per client in the system and allows you to administer, maintain and update your client-specific SAML2 applications yourself (not on the corporate Idp). This can save you a lot of time and effort to coordinate changes or onboardings of new systems/clients in your SAML2 SSO landscape. 

 

Prerequisites

Before starting, make sure you have the following in place:
  1. An SAP S/4HANA system - on-premise or private cloud.
  2. An SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) account - either a trial account or one provided by a client/organization.
  3. An SAP Cloud Identity Services subscription of type "application" on this BTP account/subaccount.
  4. Administrator rights in SAP Cloud Identity Services**, along with an established trust relationship between BTP and Cloud Identity Services
  5. A corporate identity provider (IdP). Setting up the IdP itself is not covered in depth, as there's already extensive documentation available for SAML2 setups with common providers (e.g. Microsoft Entra ID). This tutorial uses AWS IAM Identity Center as IdP, which works well for this purpose and is free with an AWS subscription.

Step 1: Enable SAML2 on S/4HANA

  1. Activate all required ICF nodes (Documentation can be found here: Configuring ICF Services for SAML2 Authentication) 
  2. Open SAP GUI and execute transaction SAML2
  3. Open the suggested URL with the path 
/sap/bc/webdynpro/sap/saml2
  • Press the Enable SAML 2.0 Support by pressing the drop-down and choose Create SAML 2.0 Local Provider
  • Provide the Provider Name and choose the pattern <SID><MANDT>, in my case A4H001
  • Move to Service Provider Settings and choose selection mode: Automatic. This will prevent a selection screen of the provider upon logon (we don't need the selection since we only have one provider)
  • Press finish for the system to generate the SAML 2.0 Local Provider Configuration
  • Press the Metadata button on the resulting dialog, check all boxes and press Download Metadata (an XML file will be downloaded)

Watch out for: The provider Name you choose becomes part of the entity ID in your SAML2 metadata. Renaming or changing its value means you have to re-download and re-upload it in Step 2. Plan your naming convention (e.g. SID+client) upfront, especially when onboarding multiple clients.

 

Step 2: Create a SAML2 application on SAP Cloud Identity Service

  1. Open the SAP Cloud Identity Service Admin UI and navigate to "Applications".
  2. Press the create button and name this application the same as your local provider 
  3. Make sure to set the Protocol Type to SAML2
  4. In the application open the SAML2 Configuration
  5. Press Load From File and choose the XML file that was downloaded in Step 1.
  6. Navigate to Conditional Authentication and choose your corporate IdP from the dropdown as Default Identity Provider.
  7. Save the configuration

Watch out for: The attributes your corporate IdP sends aren't automatically forwarded through to the SAP application on Cloud Identity Service - this needs explicit configuration. Under Trust > Single Sign-On > Attributes in the Cloud Identity Service application, make sure the correct claim from the corporate IdP is mapped and forwarded, and that the Subject Name Identifier is set correctly. If this mapping is missing or wrong, the SAP system won't receive the attribute it needs for user federation (e.g., email), and you'll get a silent failure: the user is bounced back to a password prompt with no error message.

 

Step 3: Add a Trusted Provider in the S/4HANA System

  1. Navigate back to the SAML2 webdynpro and under the tab trusted provider choose Add>Manually 
  2. Copy the tenant domain of your SAP Cloud Identity Provider (https://<tenant_subdomain>.accounts.ondemand.com) without the trailing slash (this is important) into the Name input textbox. You can extract the domain from your tenant information in SAP Cloud Identity Service. 
  3. Download the primary signing certificate from your SAP Cloud Identity Service Tenant SAML 2.0 Configuration and upload.
  4. Set Digest Algorithm to SHA-256
  5. Choose the encryption certificate and provide the same cert as for the primary signing certificate.
  6. Set Single Sign On Endpoint to the value provided in the SAP Cloud Identity Service Tenant SAML 2.0 Configuration.
  7. Do the same for the Single Logout Endpoint.
  8. Finish the dialog.

Watch out for: The trailing slash of you SAP Cloud Identity Service domain. If you copy the tenant domain out of your browser's address bar, it often comes with a trailing /. S/4HANA uses this value for entity ID matching, so that extra character is enough to make the trust silently fail to resolve. Paste the domain carefully and double-check there's no trailing slash before saving.

 

Step 4: Configure Identity Federation and User Attribute Assertion

  1. Edit the Trusted Provider we created in Step 3, choose the Identity Federation tab. 
  2. Press the Add button
  3. Choose E-mail (make sure your corporate identity provider sends this SAML Attribute to SAP Cloud IAS)
  4. Choose UserID Mapping Mode to Email (this will point to the Mail Adress in the SU01 user, you can alternatively also use the ALIAS if this contains the mail address of the user)

Watch out for: as with the NameID format issue in Step 2, an incorrect setting here fails silently - there's no clear error, just a login that bounces back to a password prompt. Double-check that the UserID Mapping Mode actually matches what's configured in the target user's SU01 record: Email, Alias, or User ID might not be set up the way you assume, especially if user provisioning was handled by a different team. Verify the actual attribute values being received using the security diagnosis tool covered later in this post - it will show you exactly what's coming through in the assertion, so you can confirm the mapping mode lines up with reality before you spend time troubleshooting elsewhere.

Step 5: Test Logon

  1. Open a private browser window and call your Fiori Launchpad URL
  2. You should be re-directed to the corporate IdPs logon page
  3. Sign in and you should be logged in to the system

 

Step 6: 

  1. Repeat steps 1-5 for as many clients as you need to onboard in this system.
  2. No additional configuration is needed on the corporate IdP side, this is all covered by a single trust relationship between SAP Cloud IAS and your corporate IdP.
  3. Verify your charged applications on SAP Cloud IAS (you can manage them centrally via the Admin UI)

 

Troubleshooting

If you are facing problems when logging in (such as logging in via your corporate IdPs logon page but still have to type in Username + Password after sign-in), your SAML2 authentication is failing silently. This can have many reasons, but the most effective way to debug this is the security diagnosis tool available under /sap/bc/webdynpro/sap/sec_diag_tool. Make sure to activate the required ICF node. Start a troubleshooting session and repeat the logon attempt. Make sure to stop the trace after your attempt and look at the log files. You will be able to see the exact SAML2 attributes the system receives from the SAP Cloud Identity Service. This way you can identify for instance if the mail attribute has been sent over correctly. 

Conclusion and Final Thoughts

Using SAP Cloud Identity Service as an identity broker between an on-premise S/4HANA landscape and a corporate identity provider turns what would otherwise be a 3×3 problem (nine separate SAML2 applications for three systems with three clients each) into a single trust relationship on the corporate IdP side. The configuration (Steps 1-4) still needs to be repeated per system and client, but it's work your own team controls end-to-end, without waiting on a separate identity team for every onboarding or change.

Limitations to keep in mind: this pattern adds Cloud Identity Service as a dependency in your authentication chain: if it's unavailable, SSO to all connected clients is affected. Make sure to configure an alternative logon method as a backup, (e.g. Client Certificate Authentication) that can be activated when SAP Cloud Identity Service is unavailable.

Next steps: once the broker pattern is working for one system, the same trust relationship extends to any additional on-premise or private cloud system you bring into the landscape: Fiori Launchpads, standalone Basis systems, or additional S/4HANA instances can all reuse the same corporate IdP trust. SAP Cloud Identity Service also offers risk-based authentication and IP-range restrictions, which are worth layering in once the base SSO flow is stable.

entry.title: MCP Server with Integration Suite, expose CAP API (SCI) via OAuth2JWTBearer Principal Propagation
entry.content:
Introduction/Scenario

This post explains how to configure an MCP server through SAP Integration Suite to securely communicate with CAP API services using OAuth2JWTBearer Assertion. This approach ensures that API access is governed through individual user identities rather than a shared API/technical user, this approach provides better governance, traceability, and compliance.

Important reference: For a detailed explanation of the JWT Bearer Flow App-to-App Authentication setup

  • SAP Help Portal | SAP Online Help
  • Consuming APIs from Other Applications | SAP Help Portal

Previous similar posts

  • MCP Server with Integration Suite, expose S/4HANA ... - SAP Community
  • MCP Server with Integration Suite via API Centric ... - SAP Community

For example, when a user interacts with an AI agent that is connected to the MCP server and accesses CAP APIs, the user should only be able to view and manage data that they are authorized to access. This access is controlled by the user's assigned policies/group under Cloud Identity, ensuring that existing security and governance policies are enforced.

Thanks @MCZL on helping and provide insight on Cloud Identity Services and BAIP/BTP Destination setup. 

 Flow:

→ Agent (Claude/Github Copilot/any AI Agent) 
  → MCP server by Integration Suite (Authenticated via IAS)
    → BTP Destination Service (OAuth2JWTBearer) 
        → CAP Service APIs (executed as the authenticated user)

Note: 

  1. The MCP server uses SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS) as its authentication provider instead of the default XSUAA, as the target APIs are also protected by SAP Cloud Identity Services. Directly accessing an IAS-protected resource through an XSUAA-based authentication flow don't seem feasible.
  2. This approach limits to a single client ID allowed to access the MCP server access This restriction exists because the BAIP/BTP destination configuration requires the consumer's client ID to be specified rather than the provider's client ID. In this scenario, the consumer is the Integration Suite MCP server, while the provider is the CAP service.
  3. However, you can directly use the provider client ID for the Integration Suite MCP and the Destination setup, skip on creating a separate SAP Cloud Identity Service instance as Consumer, however the restriction - Single client ID still applied on this. This writing is demonstrating how to use separate SAP Cloud Identity Service instance as Consumer to call the CAP API (as Provider).
  4. OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion can also be used in this scenario. However, this authentication flow is typically designed for communication between Cloud Foundry applications - SAML Bearer Assertion Flow between Cloud Foundry Applications | SAP Help Portal

Pre-requisite:

  • SAP BAIP/BTP with Cloud Foundry Enabled
  • SAP Integration Suite with MCP server, Integration Cell runtime capability
  • SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS)
  • AI Agent able to communicate with MCP server

1. CAP Services creation and deploy

This demo is using a CAP bookshop sample (without the UI deployment) as the MCP server will only access the CAP API services. 

Note: You may use any AI Model to assist on CAP app generation, ensure you connect to the CAP MCP server for more accurate response.

entry.title: Stop Clicking, Start Scripting: Automate BTP Role Collection Mapping to IAS Groups via REST APIs
entry.content:
Introduction

Picture this: a customer is going live with a new SAP BTP landscape. Their IAS tenant already has user groups set up, their role collections are defined, and all that's left is connecting the two. Simple enough: in the BTP cockpit, navigate to Security → Trust Configuration → your IAS trust → Role Collection Mappings, and add one mapping at a time.

Now imagine doing that hundreds of times.

That was the reality for one of my customers. 130 role collections, each needing to be mapped to its corresponding IAS user group. At a conservative 3-4 minutes per mapping, finding the right collection, typing the group name exactly right, saving, repeat. You're looking at close to 8 hours of repetitive, error-prone cockpit work.

As a BTP consultant, I've seen this scenario play out more than once. And every time, the frustration is the same: the platform has everything you need, yet you're stuck doing something a machine should be doing for you.

In this blog post, you will learn how to use the SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service REST API to map BTP role collections to IAS user groups programmatically, saving hours of manual work, eliminating typo-induced errors, and giving you a reusable script you can run across every environment in your landscape.

Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure you have the following in place:

  • Subaccount Administrator role collection assigned to your user in the target BTP subaccount
  • A BTP subaccount with an IAS tenant configured as a custom identity provider
  • IAS user groups already created and populated with users
  • BTP CLI installed and configured
  • A REST client for testing: curl, Postman, or Bruno all work fine
  • Node.js (v18+) for the automation script (if you're creating a Node.js script like me)

 

Let's get scripting

Step 1 — Get API Credentials via the BTP CLI

To call the XSUAA REST API, you need a client credential pair. The cleanest way to get one is directly through the BTP CLI. No service instance or service key required.

btp login --sso
btp target --subaccount <SUBACCOUNT_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

Note:  This is the current recommended approach, replacing the deprecated apiaccess XSUAA service plan. If you come across older tutorials using "cf create-service xsuaa apiaccess" that approach still works but is being phased out.

The command returns a JSON object. Save these four values, you'll need all of them:

  • clientid
  • clientsecret
  • url (the token endpoint)
  • apiurl (the API base URL)

Step 2 — Get a Bearer Token

With the credentials in hand, request an OAuth token using the client credentials flow:

curl --request POST \
--url <url> \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
--data 'client_id=<clientid>' \
--data 'client_secret=<clientsecret>' \
--data 'grant_type=client_credentials' \
--data 'response_type=token'

Copy the access_token value from the response. You'll use it as a Bearer token in the next steps.

Step 3 — Check Existing Mappings (Optional but Recommended)

Before writing anything, it's worth checking what mappings already exist for your IAS identity provider. This gives you a baseline and avoids surprises:

curl --request GET \
--url <apiurl>/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/<IAS_ORIGIN_KEY>/attributes \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'authorization: Bearer <access_token>'

Where to find the IAS Origin Key: In your BTP subaccount, go to Security → Trust Configuration and click on your IAS trust entry. The Origin Key is shown in the detail panel. It typically looks like <something>.accounts.ondemand.com.

Step 4 — Create a Single Mapping

Now for the actual mapping call. Let's do one manually first to confirm everything works before running a bulk script:

curl --request POST \
--url <apiurl>/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/<IAS_ORIGIN_KEY>/attributes \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'authorization: Bearer <access_token>' \
--header 'content-type: application/json' \
--data '{
"attributeName": "Groups",
"attributeValue": "<IAS_Group_Name>",
"operator": "equals",
"roleCollectionName": "<BTP_Role_Collection_Name>"
}'

A few things to pay attention to:

  • attributeName must be exactly "Groups" with capital G, case-sensitive. This is the single most common mistake, and it fails without a helpful error message, so double-check this first.
  • attributeValue is the IAS group name, not the group ID.
  • roleCollectionName must match the role collection name exactly as it appears in the BTP cockpit.

A successful call returns HTTP 201 with the created mapping. To verify: go to BTP Cockpit → Security → Role Collections → open your role collection → User Groups tab. Your IAS group should now appear there.

Step 5 — Scale It Up: Automate with a Node.js Script

One mapping confirmed, now let's do all 130. The script below reads a list of mappings from a JSON file, fetches a token, and loops through each entry.

Project structure:

  • mappings.json – your list of group → role collection pairs
  • map-roles.mjs – the script
  • .env – credentials (never commit or publish this!)

.env

TOKEN_URL=https://<subdomain>.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/oauth/token
CLIENT_ID=<your-client-id>
CLIENT_SECRET=<your-client-secret>
API_URL=https://api.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com
IAS_ORIGIN_KEY=<your-ias-origin-key>

mappings.json

[
    {
        "iasGroup": "BTP_ADMINS",
        "roleCollection": "Subaccount Administrator"
    },
    {
        "iasGroup": "BTP_DEVELOPERS",
        "roleCollection": "Extension Developer"
    },
    {
        "iasGroup": "CPI_OPERATORS",
        "roleCollection": "PI Business Expert"
    }
]

map-roles.mjs

import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import 'dotenv/config';

const { TOKEN_URL, CLIENT_ID, CLIENT_SECRET, API_URL, IAS_ORIGIN_KEY } = process.env;

async function getToken() {
    const params = new URLSearchParams({
        grant_type: 'client_credentials',
        response_type: 'token',
        client_id: CLIENT_ID,
        client_secret: CLIENT_SECRET
    });
    const res = await fetch(TOKEN_URL, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
        body: params
    });
    const { access_token } = await res.json();
    return access_token;
}

async function mapRoleCollection(token, iasGroup, roleCollection) {
    const url = `${API_URL}/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/${IAS_ORIGIN_KEY}/attributes`;
    const res = await fetch(url, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: {
            Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
            'Content-Type': 'application/json',
            Accept: 'application/json'
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({
            attributeName: 'Groups',
            attributeValue: iasGroup,
            operator: 'equals',
            roleCollectionName: roleCollection
        })
    });

    if (res.status === 409) {
        console.log(`Already mapped: "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    if (res.status === 404) {
        console.error(`Not found (check name): "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    if (!res.ok) {
        console.error(`Failed (${res.status}): "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    console.log(`Mapped: "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
}

const mappings = JSON.parse(readFileSync('./mappings.json', 'utf-8'));
const token = await getToken();

for (const { iasGroup, roleCollection } of mappings) {
    await mapRoleCollection(token, iasGroup, roleCollection);
}

Install the one dependency and run:

npm install dotenv
node map-roles.mjs

You'll see a clear log for every mapping: success, already exists, or failure with the exact entry so you can investigate.

Bonus: Multi-Environment Reuse

Once your mappings.json is ready, deploying to multiple environments is trivial. Re-target the BTP CLI and generate a fresh set of credentials for each subaccount:

btp target --subaccount <DEV_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

# update .env, then:
node map-roles.mjs

# next subaccount 
btp target --subaccount <QA_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

# update .env, then:
node map-roles.mjs

# and so on ...

What was an 8-hour cockpit exercise becomes a 2-minute operation per environment. Repeatable, consistent, and auditable.

 

Conclusion

The SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service API is one of those tools that, once you know it's there, you'll reach for regularly. The manual cockpit approach is fine for a handful of mappings, but as soon as you're dealing with real-world project complexity with dozens of role collections, multiple environments, repeated deployments, it simply doesn't scale.

The setup described in this post takes maybe 30 minutes the first time: prepare your mappings.json, configure the .env, run one test call to validate. After that, it's just a matter of running the script. For the customer that inspired this post, what would have been a full day of clicking was done before lunch.

If you give this a try, I'd love to hear how it works for you especially if you adapt the script or extend it to cover other security artifacts. Drop a comment below or reach out directly.

Further Resources

  • Download SAP BTP CLI – https://tools.hana.ondemand.com/#cloud
  • BTP CLI Documentation – https://help.sap.com/docs/btp/sap-business-technology-platform/account-administration-using-sap-btp-command-line-interface-btp-cli
  • btp create security/api-credential – https://help.sap.com/docs/btp/btp-cli-command-reference/btp-create-security-api-credential
  • SAP Business Accelerator Hub – Authorization API – https://api.sap.com/api/AuthorizationAPI/resource/Role_collections
  • Accessing Administration APIs of SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service – https://help.sap.com/docs/btp/sap-business-technology-platform/accessing-administration-using-apis-of-sap-authorization-and-trust-management-service
  • Map Role Collections to User Groups – SAP Help – https://help.sap.com/docs/btp/sap-business-technology-platform/map-role-collections-to-user-groups

entry.title: SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2:Setting Up Principal Propagation with OAuth2SAMLBearer Authentication
entry.content:
This is my 350th blog post, and I'm excited to continue sharing insights, experiences, and lessons learned with the community.

Introduction

When integrating SAP BTP services with SAP Sales Cloud Version 2 or SAP Service Cloud Version 2 or ESM, one of the most common requirements is ensuring that the identity of the logged-in user flows seamlessly from the source BTP application into the target SAP Cloud system. This is known as Principal Propagation.

Without principal propagation, every API call would authenticate as a technical/service user — losing all user context, audit trails, and authorization logic that depends on who is actually logged in. With it, the end user's identity is securely carried through, enabling fine-grained access control and meaningful audit logs on the SAP Sales/Service Cloud side.

This blog walks you through the complete setup using the OAuth2 SAML Bearer Assertion Flow — the recommended approach for BTP-to-SAP Sales & Service Cloud V2 connectivity.

How It Works — The Big Picture

User (logged into BTP app)
        │
        ▼
BTP Destination (OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion)
        │  ── Generates a SAML assertion carrying the user's identity
        ▼
SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 Token Service
        │  ── Validates the assertion against the trusted certificate
        ▼
Returns an OAuth2 Access Token (scoped to that user)
        │
        ▼
API Call executed as the propagated user
The trust between BTP and SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 is established by registering BTP's X.509 certificate as a trusted issuer inside the SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 tenant.

Prerequisites

  • Access to your SAP BTP Cockpit (subaccount level)
  • Admin access to your SAP Sales Cloud V2 / Service Cloud V2 tenant
  • Ability to call REST APIs on the tenant (e.g., via Postman, Bruno, or curl)

Step 1: Download the BTP Trust Certificate

  1. Log in to the SAP BTP Cockpit and navigate to your subaccount.
  2. Go to Connectivity → Destinations → Download Trust (top-right area of the Destinations page).
  3. A .pem certificate file will be downloaded.
  4. Open the file and copy only the certificate content — the block between (but not including) the header and footer lines:

-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
MIIEXzCCA0...   ← copy everything between these lines
-----END CERTIFICATE-----

Keep this certificate value handy — you'll need it in the next step.

Step 2: Configure Inbound OAuth2 Trust in SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2

SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 needs to know about BTP as a trusted SAML assertion issuer. This is done via a dedicated IAM Service REST API on your tenant.

Important restriction: Only one OAuth2 SAML Bearer Inbound Configuration can exist per tenant.

2a. Check if a Configuration Already Exists

Send a GET request to check the current state:

GET <Your-Tenant-Host-URL>/sap/c4c/api/v1/iam-service/oauth2InboundConfiguration
  • If a configuration exists with the same BTP certificate → you can reuse it as-is.
  • If a configuration exists with a different certificate → update it (Step 2b).
  • If no configuration exists → create a new one (Step 2c).

2b. Update an Existing Configuration (PUT)

PUT <Your-Tenant-Host-URL>/sap/c4c/api/v1/iam-service/oauth2InboundConfiguration/34f8b9d2-78c2-4617-bcf2-6eb36403c667
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "id": "<existing Id found in Step 2a>",
    "clientAppName": "<A meaningful name, e.g. BTP-SalesCloud-Trust>",
    "certificate": "<Certificate content from Step 1>"
}

2c. Create a New Configuration (POST)

POST <Your-Tenant-Host-URL>/sap/c4c/api/v1/iam-service/oauth2InboundConfiguration
Content-Type: application/json

{
    "id": "34f8b9d2-78c2-4617-bcf2-6eb36403c667",
    "clientAppName": "<A meaningful name, e.g. BTP-SalesCloud-Trust>",
    "certificate": "<Certificate content from Step 1>"
}

2d. Save the Response Values

A successful POST or PUT returns a JSON response like this:

{
  "value": {
    "id": "...",
    "grantType": "SAML2_BEARER",
    "nameIdType": "EMAIL",
    "spEntityId": "...",
    "audience": "<AUDIENCE>",
    "tokenServiceUrl": "<TOKEN_URL>",
    "clientId": "<CLIENT_ID>",
    "scopes": ["<SCOPE_ID>"],
    "clientAppName": "...",
    "certificate": "..."
  }
}

Note down these four values — you'll need them in Step 3:

Field Used As

audienceAudience in BTP destination
tokenServiceUrlToken Service URL in BTP destination
clientId → appears as CLIENT_IDClient Key in BTP destination
scopes[0] → SCOPE_IDScope in BTP destination

Step 3: Create the BTP Destination

Now configure a destination in your BTP subaccount that uses the inbound configuration values you just collected.

  1. Go to SAP BTP Cockpit → Subaccount → Connectivity → Destinations → New Destination.
  2. Fill in the following fields:

Property Value

NameYour choice (e.g., SalesCloudV2_PrincipalProp)
TypeHTTP
URL<Your SAP Sales/Service Cloud Tenant Host URL>
AuthenticationOAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion
Audience<AUDIENCE> from the inbound config response
AuthnContextClassRefurn:none
Client Key<CLIENT_ID> from the inbound config response
Token Service URL<TOKEN_URL> from the inbound config response
Scope<SCOPE_ID> from the inbound config response
nameIdFormaturn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress

The nameIdFormat value tells the system to use the user's email address as the SAML NameID — this is how the user identity is matched on the SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 or ESM side.

Step 4: Configure Trusted Domains in SAP BTP Authorization & Trust Management

As a final step, ensure that your SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 tenant domain is registered as a trusted domain in SAP BTP's Authorization and Trust Management service (XSUAA/SAP Cloud Identity Services).

Refer to the official SAP documentation: Configure Trusted Domains for SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service.

This ensures that SAML assertions issued by BTP are only accepted by explicitly trusted target systems — an important security boundary.

Summary

Here's a quick recap of the end-to-end setup:

Step 1 → Download BTP X.509 Trust Certificate
Step 2 → Register certificate as Inbound OAuth2 Config on SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2
Step 3 → Create OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion Destination in BTP using response values
Step 4 → Register SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 domain as trusted in BTP Auth & Trust

Once complete, any BTP application or service using this destination will automatically propagate the logged-in user's identity to SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 — without requiring users to re-authenticate or sharing technical credentials.

Key Takeaways

  • Principal Propagation bridges the identity gap between BTP and SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2, preserving the real user context across systems.
  • The trust is certificate-based — BTP's signing certificate is registered directly in the SAP Sales/Service Cloud V2 IAM service.
  • The fixed UUID (34f8b9d2-78c2-4617-bcf2-6eb36403c667) is a well-known system identifier for this configuration — don't change it.
  • Only one inbound configuration is allowed per tenant, so manage it carefully across teams.
  • User matching relies on email address as the SAML NameID — ensure users exist with the same email in both systems.

Share to your colleagues or Have questions or ran into issues during the setup? Drop them in the comments below.

entry.title: Joule A2A: MCP Gateway to S/4HANA with Principal Propagation
entry.content:
In a previous post we looked at connecting a custom A2A agent to S/4HANA Public Cloud with full principal propagation. But that approach comes with some drawbacks: hooking up individual APIs doesn't scale well, and it's hard to enforce governance. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for exposing tools and data to AI agents in a uniform way, and it's quickly becoming the common language between agents and enterprise systems. SAP's reference architecture for Agents and MCP positions Integration Suite as an MCP Gateway to safeguard traffic to enterprise systems — so this post extends the example to route a BTP-based agent through that gateway, still from customer-managed Joule.

Note: This post covers Customer-Managed Joule.

Scenario

We have an A2A-capable agent connected to Joule (customer-managed), with a destination that hands the Joule user's token to the agent on each A2A request. To reach S/4HANA Public Cloud, that agent now goes through the MCP Gateway: Integration Suite points its gateway at an S/4HANA OData service via a destination, the selected endpoints become MCP tools, and it all runs on Integration Cell. The user identity is propagated the whole way — from Joule, through the custom agent, through the MCP Gateway, into S/4HANA — so the backend call runs as the real user. And because the gateway sits on Integration Suite, we inherit the API Management controls we already know: additional authentication and authorization on top, plus IP filtering, rate limiting and quotas where we need them.

This matters because many customers have built their agents in an A2A manner, and their API policy often restricts them to endorsed architectures only.

Prerequisites

  • A working A2A agent and destination setup, as described in the principal propagation post
  • An S/4HANA Public Cloud system
  • Integration Suite, Enhanced Edition (only that Edition contains the MCP Gateway)

Step 1: Trust the Integration Suite subaccount in S/4

The very first step diverges from the previous post: the trust setup. Last time we configured S/4 to trust the destination certificate of the agent's subaccount. This time the piece that resolves the SAML Bearer assertion is the destination service of the subaccount where Integration Suite lives — and that is a different subaccount, with a different signing certificate (at least in my case). So we repeat the communication setup against that subaccount.

Concretely, in your Integration Suite subaccount go to Connectivity → Destinations → Download Trust and grab the .pem. It is a self-signed cert whose subject looks like cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/<subaccount-id> with OU=CP Destination Configuration — this is the destination-service signing certificate.

Then, exactly as in the principal propagation post, set up a communication user, a communication system and a communication arrangement (SAP_COM_0008 for Business Partner) in S/4 — but upload this certificate under the communication system's OAuth 2.0 Identity Provider, and copy its subject CN into the Provider Name field.

Note: if the trust is missing or points at the wrong subaccount, the SAML exchange later fails with a very explicit "There is no trust between entities … in client 100". That message contains the subaccount ID it actually saw, which makes it easy to tell that you trusted the wrong one.

Step 2: Create the S/4HANA SAML Bearer destination in the IS subaccount

Next, create an HTTP destination toward S/4HANA in the subaccount where Integration Suite resides. This is the same OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion destination as in the previous post — the MCP server will use it as its target. The important properties:

Name=S4_MCP_GATEWAY_TEST
Type=HTTP
ProxyType=Internet
Authentication=OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion
URL=https://my3xxxxx-api.s4hana.cloud.sap
Audience=https://my3xxxxx.s4hana.cloud.sap
Token Service URL=https://my3xxxxx-api.s4hana.cloud.sap/sap/bc/sec/oauth2/token
Client Key / Token Service User=<the comm user from step 1>
authnContextClassRef=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:X509
userIdSource=mail
nameIdFormat=urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress

# additional properties
x_user_token.jwks_uri=https://<your-ias-tenant>/oauth2/certs
IntegrationCell.Include=true

Two things that are easy to miss:

  • x_user_token.jwks_uri points at the IAS tenant so the destination service can validate the forwarded end-user token and build the SAML assertion for the real user. Without it, it silently falls back to a technical-user assertion and propagation breaks.
  • IntegrationCell.Include=true is a label on the destination. Without it the destination simply won't appear in the MCP Server wizard's dropdown at all.

Step 3: Build the MCP server in Integration Suite

Now the new part. In Design → Integrations and APIs, create an integration package to hold the artifact.

Inside the package, add an MCP Server artifact. The wizard's first step asks for the source type — pick HTTP Endpoint with OpenAPI Specification:

In the next step, point it at the S4_MCP_GATEWAY_TEST destination with a relative URL of /sap/opu/odata/sap/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER, give it a name and an MCP Path (e.g. /s4_bp_mcp), and leave the runtime profile on Integration Cell:

Skip the AI spec generation. Once the artifact exists, open its MCP Configuration → Source tab and hit Edit API Specification to supply the spec:

Import the OpenAPI/EDMX of the Business Partner service — you can download it from the SAP Business Accelerator Hub, or just pull the live $metadata from your own system:

On the Tools tab, select the operations you want to expose; each one becomes an MCP tool. I started with a single GET A_BusinessPartner → the tool get_A_BusinessPartner. Keep it small; the model routes better with fewer, well-described tools:

The tricky part is the inbound security — this is where the whole principal-propagation story lives. On the Policies tab every MCP server has a mandatory Authentication and Authorization policy, so we look at both.

Authentication

The Authentication policy decides which tokens the gateway trusts. By default an MCP server validates tokens issued through the Integration Suite subaccount's own XSUAA / the IdP configured there. That default path is enough for a client like Joule Work Desktop, which runs its own user-token fetch flow against that trusted authorization server when you add the connector — so the end-user identity is already there, you don't configure anything extra on the gateway.

Our case is different: the token doesn't come from a JWD connector, it's the JWT our A2A agent forwards from Joule, issued by our IAS tenant — and a raw token from that issuer is rejected by the default policy with 401 invalidToken because the gateway doesn't trust it yet.

The fix is to switch the Authentication policy to External OAuth (OIDC) and point it at our IAS tenant. Even though this feels a bit strange — our IAS tenant is treated as an "external" OAuth provider here — the "internal" option is the subaccount's XSUAA, which may well itself be configured to redirect logins to exactly that same IAS. So "external" just means: validate the token directly against the IAS tenant, by its own issuer and keys.

Once External OAuth is selected, there are four fields to fill:

Field Value

Well-Known URLhttps://<ias-tenant>/.well-known/openid-configuration
Audiencethe aud of the token the client actually sends (see the gotcha below)
ClientID Key${authn.oidc.jwt.azp}
UserInfo Key${authn.oidc.jwt.mail}

What these actually do: the Well-Known URL tells the gateway which IAS tenant to trust — it discovers the issuer and the signing keys from there, and validates every incoming token's signature against them. The Audience is the gateway saying "I only accept tokens that were actually meant for this application" — it's matched against the token's aud claim. ClientID Key and UserInfo Key are expressions that tell the gateway which claims carry the calling client's ID (azp) and the end user's identity (mail) — the latter being exactly the identity that gets propagated downstream.

The Audience is the one that'll bite you. Our destination maps userIdSource=mail, and the token that eventually arrives is the one Joule forwarded — i.e. after its app-to-app exchange — so its aud is the Custom Agent App client ID, not the login app you used to get a test token. You find that client ID in your IAS admin console under Applications → your Custom Agent App → Client ID (it's the same value that your agent already validates as its IAS_AUDIENCE). If you set the policy audience to the wrong app, the real Joule token is rejected with 401 invalidToken even though everything else is correct. You can also list multiple audiences comma-separated, or leave it empty to skip audience validation entirely while debugging.

If authentication is not configured correctly, the gateway rejects the call before it ever reaches your backend — a decoded IAS token that doesn't match issuer/audience comes back as:

{ "error": { "code": "invalidToken", "message": "Unable to authenticate user, invalid token" } }

(HTTP 401)

Authorization

The second mandatory policy is Authorization — and this is where it helps to understand how an IAS token is built, because it is fundamentally different from the XSUAA token you may be used to.

An XSUAA access token carries a scope claim (things like myapp.Read, API.invoke), and the default Authorization policy checks exactly that: does the token contain the required scope? An IAS token has no scope claim at all. IAS is an identity provider — it answers "who are you", not "what may you do"; the actual authorization is expected to happen in the target system (the user's S/4 roles, in our case). A decoded IAS user token has mail, sub, azp — but nothing a scope-based policy can match on.

What an IAS token does carry, because it came through Joule's app-to-app exchange, is the ias_apis claim — a list of the exposed APIs the user is allowed to call:

{
  "iss": "https://<ias-tenant>",
  "aud": "<custom-agent-app client id>",
  "azp": "<proxy-app client id>",
  "mail": "felix.bartler@sap.com",
  "ias_apis": ["a2a_custom_agent_app_api"]
}

So the configuration change versus the XSUAA default is: don't check a scope claim, check the ias_apis list instead. Point the Authorization policy's Scope Key at ias_apis and set the expected value to our exposed API:

Authorization field Value

Authorization TypeOAuth Scope OR Developer Key
Scope Keyias_apis
Scopea2a_custom_agent_app_api

The policy then checks whether the ias_apis list contains a2a_custom_agent_app_api — which doubles as a useful access gate: it enforces, right at the gateway, that only users entitled to this agent's exposed API can call it at all.

If authorization is wrong — e.g. the policy still checks scope, which an IAS token doesn't have — the gateway authenticates the user fine but then refuses the operation:

{ "error": { "code": "forbidden", "message": "User doesn't have the authorization to perform this operation" } }

(HTTP 403)

With both policies right, the gateway accepts the real Joule user token, validates it against IAS, reads mail, and forwards the identity to the destination.

Deploy MCP Server

Finally Deploy onto the Integration Cell runtime, and once the Runtime Status reads STARTED the MCP URL is live:

We've basically turned an OData endpoint into a proper MCP Server — with a curated list of tools — and put an auth layer in front of it that enforces principal propagation. Let's test it:

Testing the gateway with curl

Before touching any agent code, it's worth proving the gateway end to end in isolation — exactly like the SAML dry-run in the previous post. MCP over Streamable HTTP is just JSON-RPC over HTTP, so three curl calls do it: initialize (which returns an mcp-session-id response header you must echo back), notifications/initialized, then tools/call.

# USER_JWT = a REAL Joule-forwarded token (see the caveat below), MCP_URL = the deployed MCP server URL

# 1) initialize — grab the mcp-session-id straight from the response header
SID=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%header{mcp-session-id}' -X POST "$MCP_URL" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_JWT" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"1.0"}}}')

# 2) say "initialized"
curl -s -o /dev/null -X POST "$MCP_URL" -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_JWT" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" -H "mcp-session-id: $SID" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}'

# 3) call the tool as the user (note: OData options without `$`, select is an ARRAY)
curl -s -X POST "$MCP_URL" -H "Authorization: Bearer $USER_JWT" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" -H "mcp-session-id: $SID" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"get_A_BusinessPartner","arguments":{"top":3,"select":["BusinessPartner","BusinessPartnerName"]}}}'

This is the fastest feedback loop for getting the two policies right — the error you get back tells you exactly which stage failed: 401 invalidToken = authentication (issuer/audience), 403 forbidden = authorization (scope/ias_apis), real OData rows = success.

Getting a token that actually works for the test. A plain IAS password grant gives you a token audienced for the login app and without ias_apis, so it fails both audience and authorization — it is not a stand-in for what Joule sends. You have two options to get a realistic token:

  1. Reproduce the app-to-app exchange yourself. This is exactly what Joule does internally: take the user token and exchange it (via the jwt-bearer grant against your IAS, using the proxy app's client credentials and the proxy-to-target dependency) into a token audienced for the Custom Agent App — which then carries ias_apis. If you own the proxy app's credentials, this is the clean, scriptable way and the one I'd recommend for a proper test harness.
  2. Capture a real one. Quicker for a one-off: temporarily log the raw Authorization header in your agent, prompt Joule once, and copy the forwarded JWT out of the logs.

Step 4: The Python agent that calls the MCP gateway

The change on the agent side is small and local: the one place that used to call the destination service and S/4 directly (s4_client.py in the previous post) is replaced by a small MCP client. Everything else — the LangGraph tool, the executor, the IAS middleware on the agent's own inbound endpoint — stays as it was.

The MCP client uses Streamable-HTTP JSON-RPC to call the MCP Gateway. This is part of the standard of MCP - and one could also use a SDK. We do 3 calls: initialize (which hands back an mcp-session-id response header you carry on every following request), notifications/initialized, and tools/call:

# mcp_client.py (abridged)
def call_business_partner_api(user_jwt, top=10, select=None, filter_expr=None, ...):
    session_id = _open_session(user_jwt)        # initialize -> mcp-session-id
    r = requests.post(
        MCP_URL,
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {user_jwt}",   # <-- the whole trick
            "Accept": "application/json, text/event-stream",
            "mcp-session-id": session_id,
        },
        json={
            "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/call",
            "params": {
                "name": "get_A_BusinessPartner",
                "arguments": {"top": top, "select": [...]},   # OData options, no `$`, select is an array
            },
        },
    )
    # tool output comes back as result.content[0].text (JSON string of the OData payload)

The user_jwt it forwards is the exact same token the agent already extracts from the inbound A2A request — unchanged from the previous post:

# agent_executor.py — the token comes straight from the Authorization header Joule sent
auth = context._call_context.state.get("headers", {}).get("authorization", "")
user_jwt = auth[len("bearer "):] if auth.lower().startswith("bearer ") else None
# ... threaded down to the tool, which puts it on the MCP call as Authorization: Bearer

The key point: the agent needs no credentials of its own for the backend. No client secret, no destination binding to S/4 — just the MCP_URL of the deployed gateway. It takes the user's token and passes it on; IAS, the gateway and the destination service do the rest. (The agent's own inbound A2A endpoint is still protected by the IAS middleware exactly as before.)

Two details are worth knowing when calling an Integration-Suite-generated tool: the handshake is session-based (echo the mcp-session-id header after initialize), and the generated tool schema uses OData options without the leading $, with select/expand/orderby as arrays of strings — pass a comma-separated string and the call fails schema validation.

Test in Joule

Deploy the agent, point Joule's agent destination at it, and prompt it — e.g. "show me business partners that start with I". The full chain runs: the agent forwards the user's token to the gateway, the gateway validates it against IAS, propagates the signed-in user through the SAML Bearer destination, and S/4HANA returns exactly the records that user is authorized to see, rendered as a table in the conversation:

This is the point of the whole exercise: the data comes back scoped to the real signed-in user, propagated all the way from Joule to S/4HANA — exactly the behaviour we wanted. And because it now runs through the gateway, we can also see it happen: in Integration Suite under Monitor → Integrations and APIs → Monitor Message Processing (with the Integration Cell runtime selected), each prompt shows up as a BusinessPartnerMCP entry of type MCP Server, status Completed. That's the proof the call actually traversed the MCP gateway rather than some direct backchannel — and the governance, tracing and policy enforcement that come with it apply to every call.

Conclusion

Looks good. We have the full flow in place and can use the MCP Gateway for our A2A Agents. Hope you found this insightful.

The full code is on GitHub under a2a_pp_mcp_gateway/.

This post is part of the Joule A2A series:

  • Connect code-based agents into Joule
  • Secure code-based agents with IAS
  • Handling multi-turn conversations
  • Building custom Joule capabilities: message types in practice
  • Propagate the user identity from Joule into S/4HANA
  • MCP Gateway to S/4HANA with Principal Propagation (this post)

entry.title: Part 2 of 2 – Securing AI-Powered SAP Apps on SAP BTP: Single Sign-On and Role-Based Access with XSU
entry.content:
Overview

Part 1 of this series described how SAP S/4HANA data can be made available to AI clients through an MCP server running on SAP BTP. Once such data is exposed through a user interface, the application must meet the same security standards as any other access to SAP systems.

This article describes how a UI application on SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry runtime, authenticates users and enforces authorizations using two standard platform components:

  • Application router – the single entry point that handles user login and request forwarding.
  • SAP Authorization and Trust Management service (XSUAA) – the service that issues tokens and manages scopes, role templates and role collections.

The approach addresses three requirements:

  • Authentication: only users with a valid corporate identity can access the application.
  • Authorization: each user can access only the functions assigned to them.
  • Enforcement: authorization decisions are made on the server and cannot be bypassed in the browser.

Solution components

Component Responsibility

Identity provider (for example, SAP Cloud Identity Services connected to the corporate directory)Authenticates the user through corporate single sign-on.
XSUAAIssues a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) containing the user's scopes, based on the assigned role collections.
Application routerActs as the single public entry point. Redirects unauthenticated users to the login, maintains the user session and forwards requests to the application together with the token.
UI applicationValidates the token on every request and grants access only to the functions permitted by its scopes.

Users always access the application through the application router, and the application validates the token independently. This provides two separate layers of control.

Authentication flow

The following steps describe the first access of a user to the application:

  1. The browser requests the application through the application router. No session exists yet.
  2. The application router redirects the request to XSUAA, which delegates authentication to the configured identity provider.
  3. The user authenticates with the corporate login, typically through single sign-on.
  4. The identity provider confirms the user's identity to XSUAA. XSUAA determines the user's role collections and issues a JWT containing the corresponding scopes.
  5. The application router stores the token in its server-side session and returns the requested page. The browser receives only a session cookie.
  6. For each subsequent request, the application router attaches the token and forwards the request to the application.
  7. The application validates the token (signature, expiry and audience) and evaluates the scopes before processing the request.

 

Figure 1: Authentication flow. The highlighted arrows show where the token is transferred; it is exchanged only between server-side components.

When the session expires, the application router repeats the flow from step 2.

Authorization model

XSUAA separates the definition of permissions from their assignment through three levels:

Level Purpose Maintained by

ScopeA single permission that the application checksDeveloper, in xs-security.json
Role templateGroups one or more scopes into a functional roleDeveloper, in xs-security.json
Role collectionBundles roles for assignment to users or user groupsAdministrator, in the SAP BTP cockpit

The complete xs-security.json is shown in step 1 of the configuration below.

With this model, access is managed entirely in the SAP BTP cockpit. Granting or revoking access requires no code change and no redeployment. Assigning role collections to user groups from the identity provider, rather than to individual users, keeps access aligned with organizational changes automatically.

Configuration steps

The following examples use generic names (my-xsuaa, my-approuter, my-ui-app) and placeholders in angle brackets. Replace them with the values of your own subaccount.

Step 1: Define the security descriptor (xs-security.json)

{
  "xsappname": "my-ui-app",
  "tenant-mode": "dedicated",
  "scopes": [
    { "name": "$XSAPPNAME.Display", "description": "Use the application" },
    { "name": "$XSAPPNAME.Monitor", "description": "Use the monitoring functions" }
  ],
  "role-templates": [
    { "name": "Viewer",         "scope-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.Display"] },
    { "name": "MonitoringUser", "scope-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.Display", "$XSAPPNAME.Monitor"] }
  ],
  "role-collections": [
    { "name": "App Viewers",      "role-template-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.Viewer"] },
    { "name": "Monitoring Users", "role-template-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.MonitoringUser"] }
  ],
  "oauth2-configuration": {
    "redirect-uris": ["https://<approuter-host>.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/**"]
  }
}

Create the XSUAA service instance from this file. Later changes are applied to the same instance with update-service:

cf create-service xsuaa application my-xsuaa -c xs-security.json
cf update-service my-xsuaa -c xs-security.json

Step 2: Configure the application router

The application router is a small Node.js application based on the @SAP/approuter package. It needs three files.

package.json:

{
  "name": "my-approuter",
  "dependencies": { "@sap/approuter": "^20" },
  "scripts": { "start": "node node_modules/@sap/approuter/approuter.js" }
}

xs-app.json – every route requires an XSUAA login, and requests are forwarded to the UI application:

{
  "welcomeFile": "/",
  "authenticationMethod": "route",
  "logout": { "logoutEndpoint": "/logout" },
  "routes": [
    {
      "source": "^/(.*)$",
      "target": "/$1",
      "destination": "ui-app",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    }
  ]
}

manifest.yml – the destination ui-app points to the UI application, and forwardAuthToken passes the user's token on:

applications:
  - name: my-approuter
    memory: 256M
    services:
      - my-xsuaa
    env:
      destinations: >
        [ { "name": "ui-app",
            "url": "https://<ui-app-host>.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com",
            "forwardAuthToken": true } ]

Set csrfProtection according to your application. If the UI application implements its own CSRF protection, the router's protection can be switched off for its routes, as shown above.

Step 3: Bind XSUAA to the UI application

The UI application needs the same XSUAA instance to validate the tokens it receives. Add it to the application's manifest.yml:

applications:
  - name: my-ui-app
    services:
      - my-xsuaa

Deploy both applications:

cf push my-ui-app
cf push my-approuter

Step 4: Configure trust and assign roles

In the SAP BTP cockpit, open Security → Trust Configuration and establish trust with your identity provider. Then assign the role collections under Security → Role Collections, preferably to user groups. With the SAP BTP command line interface, the assignment can also be scripted:

btp assign security/role-collection "Monitoring Users" --to-user <user@example.com>

Server-side authorization checks

The application router ensures that only authenticated users reach the application. Fine-grained authorization is performed by the application itself, on the server, for every request:

  1. Validate the forwarded token and reject requests with a missing, expired or foreign token.
  2. Read the scopes from the token.
  3. Expose only the functions and data permitted by those scopes, both in the user interface and in the server's API responses.

Because these checks run on the server, they cannot be circumvented by modifying the page or by calling the application's API directly.

For Node.js applications, SAP provides the @SAP/xssec and @SAP/xsenv packages for token validation. A minimal example with Express:

const express = require("express");
const xsenv = require("@sap/xsenv");
const { XsuaaService, createSecurityContext } = require("@sap/xssec");

const xsuaa = new XsuaaService(xsenv.getServices({ xsuaa: { tag: "xsuaa" } }).xsuaa);
const app = express();

// 1. Validate the token on every request
app.use(async (req, res, next) => {
  try {
    req.authInfo = await createSecurityContext(xsuaa, { req });
    next();
  } catch (e) {
    res.status(401).json({ error: "Not authenticated" });
  }
});

// 2. Require a scope for a protected function
const requireScope = (scope) => (req, res, next) =>
  req.authInfo.checkLocalScope(scope) ? next() : res.status(403).json({ error: "Not authorized" });

app.get("/api/monitoring", requireScope("Monitor"), (req, res) => {
  res.json({ status: "ok" });   // only reached with the Monitor scope
});

app.listen(process.env.PORT || 8080);

For Java applications, the SAP Cloud Security Services Integration Library (java-security) offers the same functions.

Backend connectivity

User authentication protects access to the application. Communication between the application and SAP S/4HANA is a separate, technical connection through an SAP BTP destination and the SAP Cloud Connector, using a technical user. As a result, SAP S/4HANA authorizes the technical user rather than the individual end user.

This is suitable for a proof of concept. For productive use, principal propagation should be considered, so that the end user's own SAP authorizations are also applied in the backend system.

Handling session expiry in the UI

When the application router session expires, background requests (for example fetch calls) receive a login redirect or an HTTP 401 instead of data. A reload of the page lets the application router restart the authentication flow:

async function callApi(url, options) {
  const res = await fetch(url, { credentials: "include", ...options });
  const isJson = (res.headers.get("content-type") || "").includes("application/json");
  if (res.status === 401 || !isJson) {
    window.location.reload();        // the application router redirects to the login
    return null;
  }
  return res.json();
}

Key considerations

Topic Consideration

Role changesScopes are written into the token at login. After a role collection is assigned or removed, the user must log in again for the change to take effect.
Session expiryBackground requests cannot complete an interactive login. When a session expires, the application should reload the page so that the application router can restart the authentication flow.
Service updatesUpdates to the XSUAA instance must be applied with the intended xs-security.json. Verify the resulting roles in the SAP BTP cockpit after each update.
Client-side restrictionsHiding functions in the user interface does not replace server-side authorization checks.
CredentialsTechnical credentials, such as API keys, should be provided through service bindings rather than environment variables or source code.

Summary

The application router and XSUAA provide a UI application on SAP BTP with the same authentication and authorization model as any other SAP BTP application:

  • A single entry point with corporate single sign-on.
  • Permissions carried in a signed token, defined by developers and assigned by administrators.
  • Authorization decisions enforced on the server.

An application that exposes SAP data through AI therefore requires no dedicated security model; it integrates into the standard security concept of SAP BTP. Principal propagation is the logical next step to extend user-specific authorizations to the SAP backend.

entry.title: Integrating Okta with SAP Cloud Identity Services Using a Custom SCIM 2.0 Adapter on SAP BTP
entry.content:
Introduction

Recently, I was working on an identity provisioning requirement where we needed to integrate Okta with SAP Cloud Identity Services (CIS).

The idea was simple: Okta would be the source of users and groups, and SAP Identity Provisioning (IPS) would take care of provisioning those identities into SAP Cloud Identity Services.

However, during the initial analysis, we came across an authentication challenge.

The Okta environment was configured to use OAuth 2.0 with private_key_jwt authentication for accessing its Management APIs. We needed a way for SAP IPS to retrieve users and groups while supporting this authentication mechanism.

After exploring the available options, I decided to build a small adapter using Node.js and host it on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry.

The approach worked, and I thought it would be useful to share how I built it, the architecture behind it, and a few things I learned along the way.

1. Why Did I Need a Custom Connector?

SAP Cloud Identity Services provides various options for integrating identity sources and target systems.

For this particular requirement, we wanted to use a generic SCIM 2.0 source in IPS.

The challenge was that Okta's native Management APIs use a different API structure, and our authentication requirement involved OAuth 2.0 with a signed JWT client assertion.

I wanted to avoid using long-lived Okta API tokens and keep the authentication mechanism aligned with the existing security requirements.

So, instead of trying to make IPS communicate directly with the Okta Management APIs, I introduced a small integration layer.

The idea was to let IPS communicate with a standard SCIM 2.0 endpoint while the adapter handled everything specific to Okta.

This meant I could manage authentication, API calls, and data transformations in one place without making the IPS configuration overly complicated.

2. How the Integration Works

The overall architecture is fairly straightforward.

 

Here's what happens when IPS runs a provisioning job:

  1. IPS sends a request to the SCIM endpoint hosted on SAP BTP.

  2. The Node.js application authenticates the incoming request.

  3. The adapter obtains an OAuth access token from Okta if needed.

  4. It calls the Okta APIs to retrieve users or groups.

  5. The retrieved data is converted into SCIM 2.0 format.

  6. IPS receives the response and continues with its standard provisioning process.

One thing I liked about this design was that IPS didn't need to know anything about Okta's authentication mechanism.

As far as IPS was concerned, it was communicating with a SCIM-compatible source.

3. Setting Up Authentication with Okta

This was probably the most interesting part of the implementation.

For the Okta connection, I used OAuth 2.0 client credentials with private_key_jwt authentication.

Instead of passing a client secret, the application creates a JWT assertion signed with an RSA private key.

Okta validates the assertion and issues an access token, which the adapter then uses to access the Management APIs.

For this integration, the required scopes were:

okta.users.read
okta.groups.read

The token request goes to:

POST https://{okta-domain}/oauth2/v1/token

With parameters similar to:

grant_type=client_credentials

scope=okta.users.read okta.groups.read

client_assertion_type=
urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer

client_assertion=<signed_jwt>

The Okta service application also needs the appropriate administrative permissions to read the required identity resources.

Once the access token is available, the application can call the Okta APIs.

For example, to retrieve users:

GET https://{okta-domain}/api/v1/users
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

And for groups:

GET https://{okta-domain}/api/v1/groups
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

I kept the Okta authentication logic inside the Node.js application. This way, IPS only needs its own credentials to access the SCIM service.

It also makes troubleshooting easier because the Okta authentication and IPS authentication can be checked independently.

4. Building the SCIM Adapter with Node.js

For development, I used Node.js with Express.

The application essentially acts as a translator between Okta's Management APIs and the SCIM 2.0 interface expected by IPS.

The main endpoints are:

GET /scim/v2/Users

GET /scim/v2/Groups

GET /scim/v2/Users/{id}

GET /scim/v2/Groups/{id}

I also considered standard SCIM discovery endpoints, which allow clients to understand the capabilities and schemas supported by a SCIM service.

Mapping Okta Users to SCIM

Okta returns user information in its own JSON structure.

For example:

{
  "id": "00u123456",
  "status": "ACTIVE",
  "profile": {
    "login": "john.doe@example.com",
    "firstName": "John",
    "lastName": "Doe",
    "email": "john.doe@example.com"
  }
}

But IPS expects the response to follow the SCIM schema.

So, the adapter maps the Okta attributes into something like this:

{
  "schemas": [
    "urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:core:2.0:User"
  ],
  "id": "00u123456",
  "userName": "john.doe@example.com",
  "active": true,
  "name": {
    "givenName": "John",
    "familyName": "Doe"
  },
  "emails": [
    {
      "value": "john.doe@example.com",
      "primary": true
    }
  ]
}

These are sample payloads to illustrate the mapping.

The same concept applies to groups, where the adapter maps Okta group information and memberships into the corresponding SCIM attributes.

Another thing to consider is pagination.

Okta uses cursor-based pagination for its APIs, whereas SCIM commonly uses startIndex and count.

For example:

GET /scim/v2/Users?startIndex=1&count=100

The adapter needs to handle this difference so that IPS can retrieve the required records correctly.

For larger environments, pagination becomes particularly important, along with filtering, error handling, and API rate limits.

5. Deploying the Application on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry

Once the basic adapter was ready, the next step was to deploy it.

Since I was already working in the SAP BTP ecosystem, Cloud Foundry was a natural choice.

There was no need to provision a separate server or introduce additional infrastructure.

I used a standard Node.js application structure with a Cloud Foundry manifest.

An example manifest.yml looks like this:

applications:
  - name: okta-cis-scim-adapter
    memory: 256M
    disk_quota: 512M
    buildpacks:
      - nodejs_buildpack

Deployment was done using the Cloud Foundry CLI:

cf login
cf target -o <org> -s <space>
cf push

After deployment, the application was accessible through its Cloud Foundry route.

The Okta domain, OAuth client ID, signing key and other configuration values are supplied to the application through environment-specific configuration.

For production, I would recommend using a secure secrets-management approach instead of storing private keys or credentials directly in source code.

6. Connecting SAP Identity Provisioning to the Adapter

With the application running on BTP, I moved to the SAP Cloud Identity Services side.

I created a source system in SAP Identity Provisioning using the generic SCIM system connector.

The important part was configuring the source to point to the Cloud Foundry application instead of the Okta API.

An example configuration is shown below:

Property Value

Source SystemSCIM System
URLhttps://<btp-app-route>/scim/v2
AuthenticationBasicAuthentication
Proxy TypeInternet
ResourcesUsers and Groups

The adapter was configured to accept authenticated SCIM requests, and the corresponding credentials were maintained in IPS.

From there, IPS could call the adapter, retrieve the SCIM-formatted identity data, and process it using the configured transformations and target system.

The advantage here was that the provisioning logic remained within IPS, while the adapter took care of communicating with Okta.

7. A Small Issue I Faced During Testing

Of course, the first test didn't go entirely as planned.

When I initially tested the connection from IPS, I received an HTTP 401 error.

The request was reaching the application, but the adapter was rejecting it.

Initially, I was checking the Okta OAuth configuration, but the issue turned out to be on the incoming SCIM authentication side.

After reviewing the Basic Authentication configuration and correcting the credentials, the connection worked.

This was a useful reminder that there are two different authentication layers in this setup:

IPS to the SCIM adapter: Basic Authentication over HTTPS.

SCIM adapter to Okta: OAuth 2.0 with private_key_jwt.

Once the first connection was working, I was able to validate that IPS could communicate with the deployed adapter.

The next important areas for testing in a production deployment are user and group mapping, pagination, membership handling, full provisioning runs, and retry behaviour.

8. What I Liked About This Approach

Looking back, there are a few reasons why I think this architecture makes sense.

First, it keeps the integration relatively simple. The adapter does one job: expose identity information from Okta through a standard SCIM interface.

Second, the authentication logic remains independent. If something changes in Okta's authentication requirements, the changes can be handled within the adapter without necessarily redesigning the IPS source.

Third, it's reusable. Although I built it for Okta, the same pattern could be used with another identity provider that exposes its own APIs.

And finally, SAP BTP Cloud Foundry makes it easy to host this kind of lightweight integration application alongside the rest of the SAP landscape.

That said, introducing a custom component also means taking responsibility for its maintenance, security, monitoring, and API compatibility. It's worth evaluating the available standard integration options before choosing a custom adapter.

9. A Few Takeaways

This was an interesting implementation because it involved more than just configuring an identity connector.

I had to work across Okta authentication, REST APIs, Node.js, SCIM 2.0, SAP BTP Cloud Foundry, and SAP Identity Provisioning.

A few things stood out:

  • Understanding the authentication flow before starting the integration saves time later.

  • Keeping authentication and data transformation separate makes the solution easier to troubleshoot.

  • SCIM 2.0 is a useful standard for reducing dependencies on provider-specific APIs.

  • Pagination and group membership mapping deserve attention from the beginning.

  • SAP BTP can be a practical platform for building small extensions when standard integration options don't fully match a requirement.

Source Code – GitHub Repository

I've also made the connector's implementation available on GitHub for anyone interested in exploring the approach or building something similar.

The repository includes the Node.js SCIM adapter, Okta OAuth authentication handling, and SAP BTP Cloud Foundry deployment configuration.

GitHub Repository: Custom Okta SCIM Adapter for SAP Cloud Identity Services

Feel free to explore the implementation, suggest improvements, or contribute.

Conclusion

What started as an Okta-to-SAP identity provisioning requirement eventually turned into a small but useful integration project.

By building a Node.js-based SCIM adapter and deploying it on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry, I was able to bridge the authentication and API differences between Okta and SAP Identity Provisioning.

The adapter is not intended to replace standard SAP identity connectors. It's an additional option for scenarios where specific authentication or API requirements call for a custom integration layer.

I wanted to share this experience because similar challenges can come up when integrating SAP Cloud Identity Services with different enterprise identity platforms.

Hopefully, this provides a useful starting point for anyone working on something similar.

Thanks for reading! Feel free to share your thoughts or experiences with custom identity integrations in the comments.

 

Note: This article describes a custom integration approach. The example configuration and JSON payloads are illustrative and should be validated against the actual implementation before production use.
